speechtext: MINIMUM SAVING FOR TAXPAYERS IN 1974 and 1975 AS A RESULT OF BUDGET CHANGES

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. I wonder whether the minister would be good enough to clarify some confusion which exists in the minds of a number of people as a result of last night's budget, namely, that the minimum saving which will occur as a result of this budget for the 1974 taxation year for Canadians is in fact $50 and not as has been reported by a number of people $150?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for 1974 it will be $150 and for 1975 it will be $200. Obviously, in terms of the deductibility tables this will not be implemented until the deductibility tables are changed early in January.

The minister has not clarified but rather has further confused the situation. Will he correct me if I am wrong that the $100 minimum deduction was passed in the 1973 budget and all that the minister is adding in the current budget is a $50 reduction for 1974?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is perfectly right with regard to the February, 1973 budget. There was a five per cent reduction, a minimum of $100 and a maximum of $500. In the May 6 budget, the minimum was proposed to be raised to $150 for 1974. That was implemented last night in the ways and

November 19, 1974
Oral Questions
means motion. In addition, for 1975 the minimum will be raised to $200 and the maximum raised to $750.
The minister has acknowledged that there is only a $50 reduction in addition to what was proposed in the 1973 budget.
Oh, oh.

I would like him to clarify that for 1975, in contrast to what has been suggested by a number of people, the real minimal saving in terms of those who are paying taxes in 1975 is simply an additional $50 over what they will get in 1974. I would like to hear the minister's opinion on this also since he did not document what he expected in the form of inflation. Given the rate of inflation which will inevitably take place, that $50 inevitably will be eaten away by inflationary pressures. Is that the minister's opinion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is engaging in a little game of semantics here. Certainly, he will recognize that the May 6 budget was defeated largely as a result of the efforts of the hon. gentleman and his friends.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: When I entered the House last night, the minimum tax reduction, as the hon. gentleman states, was $100. I reinstated at one stroke the $50 which would have been implemented had the hon. gentleman passed the May 6 budget, plus another $50, for a minimum of $200. Two thirds of that tax reduction will apply to taxpayers at $12,000 or less.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, November 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-10, to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak in this debate I feel it is our responsibility on this side of the House to warn people in western Canada who are in the business of producing grain to watch with great attention the agreements they are entering into with regard to advance payments. We recognize the fact that this piece of legislation is generally considered to be good, but it could well be that we will be making amendments to it because there are shortcomings in the bill which should be considered in committee.
We know that the maximum rate of advance payment is $15 per acre for wheat, $18 for barley and $14 for oats. In view of the fact that this constitutes only about 10 per cent of the income from the vast majority of the land used to grow these grains, it could well be that we will have to consider this matter in committee. It seems to me that the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board is playing a game of roulette with western Canadian grain producers. I warn producers to be careful with the arrangements or agreements they make with this minister, because I consider some of his statements to be devious. One of the first things I learned as a boy when at an exhibition was that when you saw somebody with money in his hand, you had to be careful. I remember that on one occasion I learned what was probably the best lesson I ever had: a man was standing with $4 in his hand and he said to me, "If you give me $2, I will give you $4", but when I gave him $2 his $4 disappeared.
I am reminded of this story now, when the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board is bringing in legislation to advance to individual prairie grain the sum of $15,000. We must realize, also, that this amount is multiplied for two or three producers. This is as it should be, because agricultural operations are becoming much larger. However, one of the shortcomings in the game the minister is playing is that inevitably the initial payment for grain each year is much lower than it should be. A case in point was this year.
Yesterday the minister rose in his place and increased the initial payment, and rightly so. There is no reason in the world why there should not be such a reasonable payment at the beginning of the crop year. There would not, then, be any reason for an interim payment. The minister always seems to be handing out a little bit of candy as you would to a youngster. I can assure the minister that the producers in western Canada do not wish to be treated like children: it would be wise for him to recognize that they do not appreciate this. There is no reason why the minister cannot make a fair assessment, at the beginning of the crop year, of the vicinity the final

payment will be in. He should at least be able to give the producers 75 per cent of the final payment initially, and I am sure the producers would be happy with it.
It would be in the best interests of the producers, the grain companies and the Canadian Wheat Board, as well as members of the House, if the minister would take it upon himself to increase the initial payment to 75 per cent or 80 per cent of what he anticipates the final payment will be. Of course, the minister juggles around with the final payment. If there should be an election in the current year he will grant it early, but if there is no election he will hold it back until a later date.
The deviousness of the minister was evident yesterday when he suggested in the House that the income of western producers was increasing at a phenomenal rate. He said that the increase in the first three quarters of last year was 90 per cent in the province of Saskatchewan. Perhaps it was, if he wants to use percentages, but he did not tell members of the House on what he was basing his percentage.

Cash receipts only, my colleague says. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) has stated, the income of the western grain producer is still far below that of other people in the industry. Even the grain handlers are making far more than the prairie grain producers, so I do not think it is exactly cricket when the minister uses percentages. It would be far better, far more honest, if he used the dollar value, because this is what should be recognized.
Also, the minister is trying to push through committee the two-price system for wheat which was dealt with in Bill C-19. We have reservations about that legislation. There were weaknesses in that bill and we notified the minister of an amendment we were going to put forward. In all these cash transactions the prairie grain producer must exercise a great deal of caution in dealing with the minister. At a Grains Council meeting in Edmonton not too long ago, the minister started meddling with the Crowsnest freight rate. Now he is putting forward another piece of candy for the prairie grain producer. He says he will give the grain producer a subsidy if he, the minister, will be allowed to juggle the Crowsnest freight rates.
I warn grain producers to watch the manoeuvring of this minister because they must remember that the candy might disappear. I suggest that one of the prime responsibilities of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), who represents a large wheat growing area, is to cast a scrutinizing eye on what the minister is doing, and to at least help us on this side of the House to keep the minister within bounds. Then we come to the matter of stabilization on which the minister said he will bring in a bill. He will tak" a dollar from the grower and the government will put in a couple of dollars. Mr. Speaker, I suggest it would be a good idea if the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) got together and worked out a policy on crop insurance in lieu of a stabilization bill. When the Minister of Agriculture brought in his crop insurance bill, it was supposed to resolve all the problems of agriculture-but it did not go far enough. The Minister of
November 19, 1974

Agriculture did not accept our suggestions nor, apparently, did he accept any from the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. Surely, if the two ministers put their heads together they could present a policy that would be for the benefit of agriculture in Canada, especially western agriculture.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that stabilization will establish another large bureaucracy for this country. Last night in his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) hinted at a freeze on the size of the civil service, but there is no denying the fact that one of the largest bureaucracies that western Canada has known would be required to implement a stabilization bill. This is the area where the minister should co-operate with the Minister of Agriculture to bring in one all-encompassing program for the benefit of all. As things stand now, some farmers will be in the crop insurance program, some in the stabilization program-if they accept it at all-and probably some farmers will not be in either.
Next comes the farm credit program which is to be enlarged. There is the danger that it will involve farmers in such a large amount of debt that they will never get out of it. Some years ago a former minister of agriculture who is now a member of the other place prophesied that the time would come when those who operated farms would not own them. As a westerner and one who has, with a good wife, raised a family on a farm, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it will be the saddest day Canada has known if we reach the point where the farm operator is not also the owner. We just have to consider what is happening in Russia in this regard: at the present time, 15 per cent of agricultural production comes from the 3 per cent of the land allocated to the operators. This should be a lesson for us, Mr. Speaker. No program should ever be initiated in this country that would take ownership of the farm away from the operator.

I have to report to my producers, and they tell me that $70 million is a lot of money. The western grain producer has to be careful not to get too far in debt, because financing is available to him and his margin of profit is so small that he will not be able to pay off his debt. We were dealing with grain inspectors. At present the elevators in my area are plugged. We are on a three-bushel quota and grain producers find it difficult to deliver grain while people on the other side of the world are dying of hunger. This government sits on its fanny and does nothing to improve transportation to reduce the amount of grain in our elevators. Farmers rely on advance payments because grain does not move. They need money to pay taxes and to pay grocery bills. They, too, are consumers. It costs them as much to live as it costs any

other consumer in Canada. That is why we must chastize this government: it is not moving grain as efficiently as it ought to be moved.
Farmers need extra money with which to buy fertilizer, the price of which has also been inflated. Fertilizer prices have risen from $103 to $163 for 11-48. That is a 60 per cent increase in one year. In addition, machinery prices have increased this year by approximately 30 per cent. The price of land has doubled, not because it is in demand for agriculture but because outside money has pushed up the price. Only if those engaged in agriculture can make even a modest profit will some land continue in use as agricultural land. Without a modest profit, farmers cannot stay in business.
Advance payments are not the answer. They have nothing to do with profits. Every cent of the advance must be repaid. The minister himself said that 99.9 per cent of advances over the years have been repaid. What else should we expect? Does he not realize that he has been dealing with farmers, who are honest. This money must be paid back. He has asked the grain companies to administer this program. Is this fair ball? He has asked them to distribute money and to collect it. When the Minister of Finance asks the banks to sell bonds, he rewards them. The banks do not worry about collecting money.
Under the present program, however, the grain company or the elevator agent is accountable after five years for money not collected. That is, they are accountable for the debt outstanding. There are bound to be some people who find it hard to pay because of unforeseen circumstances. I say this is a very important question on which we should spend some time. Does it matter if the agent is accountable for 10 per cent of outstanding debt or for one-quarter of 1 per cent of total advance payments? By giving him that responsibility, are we playing fair ball? The government is asking these agents to advance money to farmers. In return they will receive nothing except the goodwill of those whom they serve. We must examine this aspect of the bill in committee.
Surely the minister will be fair. He may even consider the suggestions of members from western Canada which could be of fundamental importance to western Canada and all grain producers. After all, we want to continue grain production at its maximum. If it were not for our grain, our balance of payments in Canada would be in terrible shape and Canadians would not be enjoying their present benefits. But for our exports of agricultural products and natural resources our trade balance would be one of imbalance. No country can long survive under such conditions.
Therefore, I urge the minister to consider the proposals we shall bring forward on behalf of prairie grain producers. We want to facilitate passage of this bill. We are not trying to filibuster: we merely wish to demonstrate some of the shortcomings of this bill and impress upon the minister and his colleagues how important these issues are to grain producers. We shall look after the interests of the prairie grain producers as long as we are able to stand on our feet and voice disapproval of policies which we do not think are in the best interests of all concerned.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad of this opportunity to voice my concern about agriculture. This bill deals with one aspect of agriculture, the provision of advances to grain producers for wheat stored on the farm. It has been generally accepted that the principle behind this legislation has been useful. Although this bill will be useful, I suggest that its usefulness will be limited. Why, Mr. Speaker? The agricultural industry is now working under conditions of deep distress. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) occasionally expresses interest in the plight of agriculture, but apparently he is not supported by his cabinet colleagues. This was made abundantly clear in last night's budget speech which did not contain a single reference to incentives or assistance to farmers in any part of the country. That was deplorable. I think the government ought to be ashamed of that omission, especially in view of the importance of agriculture to the well-being of this country.
The bill we are considering is designed to increase the amount of cash which may be advanced to a wheat producer. It will assist him until he must repay the cash advance. For that reason I suggest that the bill is one of limited usefulness. The basic difficulty facing our farmers stems from the fact that the government which has been in power most of the time since confederation has taken no interest in agriculture. This government has acted in accordance with a report on agriculture which was produced several years ago. That report suggested that surpluses of agricultural commodities which could not be disposed of were responsible for the difficulties facing farmers. The government then decided that the obvious answer was to reduce the number of farmers on the land and most of its agricultural policies were aimed at reducing the number of farmers. Once farmers were taken off the land the government did not need to worry about their income. That basic policy has been detrimental to this country. It must be changed or thrown out because it has not helped Canadian farmers.
In the five-year period 1956-61, approximately 95,000 farm families left the land. In the next five-year period, 1961-66, when a Conservative government was in power, because of the great interest which that government took in agriculture the rate of farm depopulation decreased- only 50,000 farm families left the land. Significantly, between 1966 and 1971, when the Liberals were back in power, rural depopulation escalated and 65,000 farm families left the land. These figures speak for themselves: I do not need to elaborate on them.
We have to ask ourselves how long this kind of depopulation can continue before this country is in the position where it can no longer produce enough food to feed its own people. I think the answer is, "Not very much longer." Indeed, in 1969, for the first time in the history of this country, there were many areas of agricultural production in which we did not produce enough to feed our people. We had to depend upon imports to supply our needs- imports which this country is well equipped to produce: I am referring to meat, dairy products, poultry products and sugar, commodities we are well able to produce.
We witnessed no particular action by this government to relieve that situation. Instead, we have had general poli-

November 19, 1974

cies, on a continuing basis, designed to create disincentives to our farmers. An example of this is the LIFT program. At that time, the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, the minister from Saskatchewan who at least theoretically should be familiar with agricultural problems, visited his rural constituents and found they had a lot of wheat in their bins. It so happened at that time Canada was having difficulty disposing of its wheat. In his wisdom, the minister decided not to seek markets but to pay farmers to stop growing wheat. That was somehow supposed to help farmers. The minister's thinking was that if you reduce the farmer's income by 100 per cent in one year, it does not matter as long as he does not have any wheat in his bin which the minister has to worry about disposing of.

Figures were provided to me by Statistics Canada for 1970, 1971, 1972 and, I think, 1973. They show that total wheat production was not up to the level which was achieved prior to the LIFT program. The LIFT program was followed by another brainchild of the minister responsible for the Wheat Board. It had the same goal: reduce the production of grain. That was the grass incentives program. Those two programs combined have almost destroyed western agriculture as we once knew it. If the minister responsible for the Wheat Board is honest and sincere, I do not think he will say to the House and the people of this country that those two programs were useful to western agriculture. He cannot say that either of those programs has stopped or even decreased the depopulation of rural areas that is taking place at this time. He cannot say that either of those programs caused the farmer to say, "Yes, there is a great future in agriculture. I will stay on the farm and encourage my children to do the same."
In his opening remarks the minister made reference to the great incomes which farmers are now receiving. It was less than honest, to say the least, to suggest that farmers' incomes are substantially better than they were 20 years ago. I have some figures for individual items. I will first
Grain
deal with the price of oats. In 1952, 22 years ago, the price was 76 cents a bushel. In 1964, ten years ago, it was 62 cents a bushel. In that twelve-year period the price decreased by 14 cents a bushel. During that time farm costs did not go down by that percentage; in fact, they increased. In 1972, oats sold for 89 cents a bushel. For 1973-74 the price is $1.03 a bushel. This represents an increase in farm income, insofar as oats are concerned, of approximately 25 cents a bushel over the past 22 years.
In 1951, wheat sold for $1.55 a bushel. In 1962, it was $1.66 a bushel; and in 1972, $1.86. The figure for 1973-74 is $3.50. In the 20-year period 1952 to 1972 the price of wheat per bushel dropped from $1.55 to $1.35-20 cents a bushel. Can the minister tell me of any farm cost that went down a similar amount in that 20-year period? I challenge the minister to show me where farm costs were reduced during that period.
I now wish to deal with live beef sold at the stockyard. In 1951, the price was 28 cents a pound; in 1961, 19 cents a pound; and in 1971, 29 cents a pound. That is one cent a pound more than in 1951, over 20 years ago. I challenge the minister to show me where the cost of producing beef has decreased or even stayed the same during that 20-year period. The figures today are a little higher. However, the report of Mrs. Plumptre, chairman of the Food Prices Review Board, indicates that although the price the beef producer receives for his product is better than it was 20 years ago, he is still selling beef between 5 and 10 cents a pound, live weight, below the cost of production. I do not think the policies this government has put forward over the past two years in so far as beef is concerned have done very much to stimulate the industry. The government has not put forward anything to encourage beef production: indeed, everything that is happening does exactly the opposite.
The beef producer is in absolute despair at this moment. Many are dispersing their herds because there is no profit in beef production. We have read in the press in the last couple of weeks that farmers were slaughtering their animals to emphasize to the public of Canada the desperate plight they are now facing because of complete lack of action by this government to assist them in keeping the industry viable. I am concerned about keeping agriculture viable. That must be the concern of us all. Where will this country go if we continue to face policies which take people away from the land, create disincentives toward production and end in loss rather than profit? Keeping animals alive on the farm actually costs the farmer money now that he cannot sell them even for as much as it costs him to raise them. So I ask, where is this country going? I should like to know the answer to that question.
Let us now consider farm costs. I have spoken at length about farm incomes, which the minister gleefully said were so great at the moment. I have pointed out that over a 20-year period farm incomes basically have not changed. However, it can be readily pointed out that farm costs have tripled, quadrupled or even more over the same period. So where is the justice in this just society of the present Liberal regime? People are slaving away for long hours, summer, spring, winter and fall, producing food to feed this country and, indeed, to feed many parts of the

As a matter of fact, I think it is fair to say that our farmers are probably the most hard working people in the country, when looked at in terms of hours put in to keep their businesses going. I ask the minister to show me which other group in this country, or indeed in North America, would be willing to work for one year for that kind of wage. I do not think he could do so. I should like to give a couple of examples of the kind of costs farmers are facing. Let me take the tractor that is equipped to pull a three-bottom plow, if I may put it in its simplest terms. In 1950 such a tractor sold for between $2,000 and $2,500. Five years ago it was selling for $5,000 to $6,000. I do not know what it is selling for today because of rapid increases, but I think it is around $10,000. This means that while farming income has basically stayed the same over a 20-year period, the cost of the basic implement of power on the farm, the tractor, has tripled or quadrupled.
Other farming costs, such as fertilizer, twine, barbed-wire and machinery parts have similarly doubled, tripled, quadrupled or increased even further during the past 20 years. Indeed, we do not need to go back that far; this increase has taken place within the past two or three years. The government indicated some small interest in this problem not too long ago when it appointed the Barber commission to study the prices of farm machinery. The commission made a report which included several recommendations. The Minister of Agriculture, in response to a question about a year ago, informed the House that he had implemented all of those recommendations but one, which I think was the one dealing with a tax on the profit made by farm machinery companies. The same minister has been asked since that time to tell us the effect of his implementation of these recommendations. Either he did not implement any of the recommendations or the recommendations were of absolutely no value in terms of keeping down the price of farm machinery.
I have already mentioned the beef producers. There seems to be some confusion on the part of the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) about what the policy really should be. On one hand the Minister of Finance says we should increase production, though the events of recent weeks and months suggest the very opposite to producers. Indeed, as I have said before, many producers are in the process of dispersing their herds. Many questions have been asked during the past few days about how the beef producers can be assisted, but the only answer we have had was from the Prime Minister today. He said he had sent some sort of note to the United States, which I presume was a protest note but

which he refused to table or to divulge to the members of the House when asked to do so. I think that is a pretty feeble effort in dealing with a crisis situation, as feeble an effort as made by the minister responsible for the Wheat Board when the international grains arrangement ran out. The effort was so feeble that no international agreement was reached on the price of grain and no effective action was taken in terms of dealing with United States policy on the importation of Canadian beef.
If the minister, who considers himself the Messiah of agriculture-he told me that personally, using those exact words-is as good as he thinks he is, why has he not taken the opportunity of going to the United States to talk about the beef situation? Instead, he sits back and does nothing except to say that some day a stabilization program will be brought in. I do not think that kind of statement does very much to encourage farmers to stay in business. It does not help the cow-calf operator who is now faced with winter and no feed to winter his calves. If he disposed of them he would do so at a loss. This is why he is waiting impatiently for some solution from the government that was so recently given a mandate.
So, Mr. Speaker, basically we must do two things if agriculture is to survive. First, more aggressive and effective action must be taken to increase farm incomes. On the other side of the coin, more aggressive and effective action must be taken to decrease or at least stabilize farm costs. During the last election campaign we proposed a solution to this problem. I am not saying it was necessarily the best solution, but it was a solution. We proposed the placing of controls on farm costs. Indeed, we proposed placing controls on farm costs nearly a year ago. If our advice had been taken a year ago, I can say quite sincerely that our farmers today would be suffering nowhere near the distress they are suffering at the moment.

The fact is that to date nothing has been done by this government to keep farm costs down. No matter what their promises have been-promises of an anti-profiteering bill or anything else-nothing has been done and farming costs continue to accelerate at a rate which is absolutely unacceptable. As long as this minister, the Minister of Agriculture and this government continue to follow do-nothing policies or policies designed to discourage production, the agricultural industry in this country will continue to decline, with its only hope for the future being continued depression and despair.
I do not know what we must do to impress upon the minds of this minister, the Minister of Agriculture and the government, that drastic action is required in agriculture today. We can talk about promises and we can listen to them; we can listen to the minister commenting on problems in other countries of the world-but none of this really comes to grips with the agricultural problems of this country and none of it is helping our farmers to survive. It is time the minister and his colleagues reassessed the situation. It is time they realized Canada must remain self-sufficient in food production and, in addition, that we must remain a major food supplier for the world.
The World Food Conference in Rome, which dealt with massive food shortages in many parts of the world, has just concluded. This is an area into which Canada can fit extremely well, because if there is anything this country can do well, it is in the field of food production. All we need are policies from this government which will encourage food production, assure a reasonable return to the producers and assure some kind of long-term stability. If we can guarantee these things to the farmers of this nation, their long-term survival will be assured.
One of the things we might also consider-this goes hand in hand with my suggestion-is that more of our foreign aid should be given in the form of food, since producing food is one of the things we do best. I make that suggestion in conclusion, Mr. Speaker. I hope the minister responsible for the Wheat Board will consider the suggestions I have made. I noticed him making notes: I am sure he will take them home and study them carefully. During the remainder of this session I expect to see legislation dealing with these matters to the benefit of the Canadian farmer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not be long in my comments on Bill C-10. However, I would like to make one or two points, first on the legislation itself and then on the whole area of grain production in Canada. Most members of the House would agree that increasing cash advances from $6,000 to $15,000 is a step in the right direction. It has been said-and it is certainly true-that inflation has hit farming in Canada, specifically in western Canada, as hard as it has hit any segment of our society. One might suggest that the increase in cash advances is a partial buffer against further inflationary rates and it can be assumed that members on this side will not be opposed to the legislation when it comes to a vote perhaps on third reading.
One matter about which we must be concerned is that of providing a guarantee, a floor price or an intervention price in respect of grain production. We hear continually from people engaged in grain production about what will
Grain
happen if the world market price drops. At the present time it looks as though grain prices will remain stable at least until 1977. One of the more important pieces of legislation to be brought in for scrutiny in the House of Commons is the grain stabilization bill, if and when it is presented.
From the little we on this side have seen of the grain stabilization bill I can only make two comments. Firstly, if the government is including all grains under this grain stabilization bill in respect of payments, I think that would be wrong. Secondly, if the government clings to its $25,000 limit as the total amount that can be accumulated by any one producer, that is totally and completely unrealistic having regard to the grain prices we are experiencing at the present time. We are all looking forward to a close examination of the grain stabilization legislation when it comes before us and, hopefully, we can make that legislation more acceptable and more in tune with the agricultural situation which now exists.
One thing I should like to refer to which is of concern to a lot of people in western Canada is this: we in the west, because of our energy resources and our agricultural potential, have a considerable responsibility to feed Canadians and other people around the world. At the present time we have high input costs in agriculture. Some examples are fertilizer, chemicals and fuels. Labour costs have also increased significantly, as have the costs of machinery and land.
If we are to maintain the kind of production required in present world circumstances, we must expand production in the area of grain. The one major problem that we are faced with in this regard is the problem created by increases in agricultural input costs. If the price protection the government proposes is not realistic in terms of dollar values, then we could conceivably have a reduction or cutback in grain production because of a reduction in the number of acres seeded to grain. If a farmer can make money by seeding a given number of acres, why should he expand the number of acres and take that added risk unless he is sure there will be a reasonable return to cover the extra risk involved? Consequently, unless something is done in a positive manner we could conceivably see a reduction in the actual number of acres used for the production of grain. I think this would be very detrimental to agriculture in Canada and to our balance of payments as a country.
The minister spoke about the positive aspects of what is taking place at the present time, and there are many. However, there are two or three uncertainties so far as grain is concerned. One is the whole aspect of transportation. No meaningful conclusion has been reached concerning the direction our transportation industry in Canada is to take. Discussions, meetings and studies have been undertaken, but there is still no clear path concerning the direction transportation is to take in western Canada. We are still at the point where we speak about inland terminals and whether there should be more, about the trackage situation at Vancouver and about whether the whole concept of grain elevator rationalization should continue.

The government has given no indication of its intention in respect of the abandonment procedure. The deadline for this will be within the next month. The whole question of grain transportation and the direction it will take in the latter part of the 1970s and into the 1980s is rather vague. This creates many uncertainties so far as the western agricultural producer is concerned. Another matter closely coupled with transportation is the Crowsnest pass rates. I believe the minister has been sending out feelers in the form of recent statements about what the government might like to do. At the resent time the government is not doing anything. In other words, the government'is running a flag up the flagpole to see which way the wind is blowing. Rather than making positive statements, the government is making overtures. This creates uncertainties in the area of grain transportation.
When we speak of the Crowsnest pass rates we are speaking about something which is fundamental and almost a basic way of life. If the government feels that a change is necessary, it should state what is to be done in return for the removal of the Crowsnest pass rates. I think this is the type of thing the farmers will be looking for.
Another matter of frustration, contention and uncertainty is the movement of grain at both our grain ports- Vancouver and Thunder Bay. The longshoremen once again are talking about a strike and the grain inspectors, from the information I receive, are almost sure to go on strike in the very near future unless they receive the kind of pay increase the grain handlers received some months ago. There are examples of the types of uncertainties that exist at the present time. The government has not taken the lead in respect of these uncertainties, and in fact has left this matter basically to the grain industry. While this is not bad, still the government must assume the major role and be the major catalyst in this whole affair because decisions will have to be made in connection with transportation, the Crowsnest pass rates and, ultimately, labour.
These matters will have a great effect, not just for the next year but certainly for the remainder of this decade. Therefore, it is very crucial that at this time leadership is shown by the government. I expect that the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board will have to assume a major portion of the responsibility in this situation.
In the area of the amounts and kinds of grain we have on hand in Canada, it is well known that the yield of the 1974 crop was disappointing. There was a decline in the grades of grain and a great proportion of it would fall into the category called utility. Because of this, I think prices will remain high for the foreseeable future, certainly into 1977 and perhaps even into 1978. An example of our supply situation is that the Canadian Wheat Board is to sell down so that it virtually has no grain left on hand. I think this is a commendable aim. It certainly is satisfactory at the present time.
Because of the quality of the grain, and because the price is remaining strong in respect of wheat in Canada- well into the $6 level-I think it must be pointed out to consumers well in advance that for the next few months, or possibly the next couple of years, they will have to pay higher prices for food in Canada. If the price of grain is

high to the livestock, hog, cattle and poultry industries, this will affect the price of other commodities. I think the consumer will have to bear with the agricultural industry in this case and be prepared to accept higher consumer prices for food.
In conclusion, I should like to say that the increase from $6,000 to $15,000 in Bill C-10 in respect of cash advances is certainly welcome. I would caution the government, however, that if it should be found at some point that there is a downturn in the rain market-although this is not likely- the $15,000 limit may not be high enough. If farm input costs in respect of producing grain gallop along as they have, it will not take much of a downturn in the end price before farmers will be in a financial position similar to the one they were in during 1969, 1970 and 1971. If this situation should arise, I hope the government will be prepared to introduce an amendment to this legislation in order to increase the limit to more than $15,000, which would be more in line with the costs being incurred by farmers.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few comments on this bill. I support its general thrust: I believe it is recognition of the fact that the cash advance idea put forward by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was feasible. I remember in the discussions of 1957 that the Liberal government of the day felt that cash advances were not a good thing, that farmers would make off with the money or that the money would not be collected in substantial amounts. It has been proved that these fears were unfounded, and now we have an expansion of these advances more in keeping with the present situation.
So I agree in principle with the bill. However, I wish to make a few comments about the necessity of the elevator agent being a collector for the government. I feel that this situation should be looked at and that someone other than the agent might well be in charge of collecting accounts, particularly where there are disputes or in cases where the individual concerned may be in difficulty. The elevator agent is in a difficult position. He is an agent of the company, which very often is the pool or the United Grain Growers. He is also an agent of the Canadian Wheat Board and must interpret what is meant by the board's regulations, and so on. He must act as arbitrator in respect of grades.
In other words, he is caught in the cross-fire between his employers, the government-through the Wheat Board- and the Grains Commission, and he attempts to satisfy his customers and often his friends and the people with whom he lives in the community. Therefore, while there do not seem to be many accounts that are delinquent for a long time, it seems important that if possible these problems should be removed from the elevator agents and taken over by someone else. Surely, in the hierarchy of people who look after the grain growers some group might be found which would be better equipped than the elevator agents to cope with this problem.
Now I should like to turn to a few other matters that are related to this bill, although not directly. One is the budget. Last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) spent a great deal of time telling us that we should grow
November 19, 1974

more grain, and I think he almost used the expression that Canadians were living too high off the hog. I do not want to expand on this subject, but it seems to me there was nothing in the budget last night for farmers, for the grain handling system. Perhaps there was a little in it for the flour processors, but there was practically nothing for the individual farmer or grain grower. In the last six years there has been a steady erosion of the tax position of grain farmers in the provisions concerning straight line machinery depreciation and the basic herd for cattlemen. We are faced with the fact that the outlook for the world is not very good. One thing which we will be able to grow and which we can export is grain, but not beef in quantities. After 70 years in which Canada has been growing grain, at least wheat will be king in the next few years. Our ability to grow and to export grain is dependent to some extent on what is in this bill.
The next subject on which I would like to speak is the settlement by the government of the grain handlers' strike. I would like to comment on this matter because in the curling rinks, the coffee bars, the pool meetings and UGG meetings across the west everyone wonders whether the federal government is ready to nationalize the grain handling system, particularly the terminals. Perhaps it is not generally known that most of the terminals are owned by the grain handling companies and are in the hands of the western co-operatives. I think it was forgotten when we put through the grain handling bill that the farmers on the prairies own these terminals. As an official of the grain handling pool said to me, "If they take away our terminals, they will be taking away the guts of our system and then we might just as well give up the country elevators".
I was impressed by an article which appeared in the Toronto Star, written by Mr. Ed Finn, public relations director of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers. In this article he presents a unionist's point of view on the grain situation. I do not think Mr. Finn knows too much about the grain handling business, but I think he was expressing a point of view that is prevalent in the country. I think it is a mistaken point of view and perhaps Mr. Finn is somewhat uninformed, but I believe it will bring to the attention of the government, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) in particular, that bad relations at the grain handling end cannot be solved by nationalizing terminals and thinking that everything will then be all righ.t. Mr. Finn suggested that our attention span with regard to labour matters is momentary and we forget about them as soon as a dispute is settled. Nevertheless, the after effects in Vancouver are still with us.
It is important to look at the facts. At the moment we have the demands from the Thunder Bay terminal union which are up for negotiation. These not only include the fringe benefits gained by the Vancouver workers, but $2 an hour in wages in the first year and $1 an hour in the second year of a two-year contract. This compares with the 87 cents and 65 cents legislated for Vancouver and would put the Thunder Bay workers far ahead of their Vancouver counterparts. This is an unheard of wage relationship when judged by any previous experience. I think the pool elevators and the UGG did realize that the demands would be high because of the Vancouver labour
Grain
settlement, but the Minister of Labour kept reiterating that the Vancouver settlement would not be a benchmark on which to base settlement of disputes of other workers in the grain handling industry. The situation is very clear in the minds of Thunder Bay workers and their representatives and it will be a long time before the aftermath of that situation is over. Furthermore, Mr. Finn said in Vancouver that the four grain elevator companies and local 333 of the grain workers union have never been able to negotiate a contract voluntarily. There is no reason to be optimistic about their next confrontation.
It has been suggested in this House, and indeed throughout the country, that over the years grain handling companies have not negotiated in good faith. I think that is inaccurate, Mr. Speaker, and just helps to create an unhealthy atmosphere. It is agreed that the relationship between union representatives and the Vancouver management group is not good, but I do not think there is a hostile relationship between the men and the supervisory staff. At the UGG, 800 loads a day have been handled since October 11. Prior to that time only 300 or 400 loads a day were handled, so it would appear that relationships between management and the union are pretty good at that terminal. The government appointed Mr. Justice Bayda to look into the grain handlers' dispute, and his findings may be of some help.
The longshoremen will soon be entering into negotiations on their contract. The main difference between the longshoreman's role and that of the grain handler is that he does not work regularly and so traditionally has received a higher rate of pay. We must realize that although this bill will help to some degree, we will have to face interruptions in the supply of grain to world markets because of the demands of unions as they attempt to keep up with the cost of living. Another consideration is the budget measures which were announced last night, which will certainly increase inflation. Mr. Finn also made an observation, which has gained wide credence, to the effect that grain co-operations are almost entirely to blame for the problems on the west coast and at Thunder Bay. This is the impression given by the appointment of Mr. Justice Bayda by the Minister of Labour.
There has been a lot of talk about the nationalization of grain terminals. However, this is not the solution unless the government intends to give in to every request made by the grain handlers' union. The government has not had much success in handling its own employees-and I make this statement with regard to any government. The problem of the federal postal employees comes to mind, and also the problem of the federal grain inspectors who must clear the grain through Vancouver harbour. If the government should take over the grain terminals, it is likely that they would grant the grain handlers a raise in pay every time they demanded one, because the money would not come from the taxpayers but from the handling charges paid by farmers. We must rid ourselves of the notion that grain must be moved at all costs. There may well come a time, Mr. Speaker, when it is just too expensive to move grain and union wage demands must be resisted. Mr. Finn made a statement which I believe to be wrong but which received wide coverage. He said:

But the grain companies wanted to have a settlement imposed on them, so they could blame added costs on the government and claim further federal subsidies.
It is his view that governments would be more free with settlements if they owned the elevators, because they would be using the farmers' money and not government money. There is also widespread belief that the federal and other governments are involved in subsidizing grain handling. But this is not the case, Mr. Speaker. Any wage increase must come out of the handling charges paid by farmers. I raise this matter because I believe the western farmer is uneasy that the grain terminals may be taken away from him and nationalized, leaving him completely at the mercy of the government. Some western farmers feel they are too involved with the government already; that government is trying to tell them what to do and is not allowing them to work out their own problems.
I support this bill in principle, Mr. Speaker. I believe it will help the farmer to plan the difficult operation of moving grain from his farm to consumers across the oceans; but we must remember that there are many other people involved who can stop the flow of grain.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on Bill C-10 from which farmers across this country may expect to receive some benefit. It is a bill that was first introduced in this House some 17 years ago by a different government, and while the objectives and philosophies seem to be the same, the motives have changed. It seems to be an attempt to keep pace with the feed grains policy-a policy which has not worked as well as it should. I should like to make it clear at the start, Mr. Speaker, that a cash advance is not a hand-out to farmers. The publicity that is so often associated with such a proposition might give people the impression that farmers are getting something from the government for nothing. Perhaps the minister could clarify this and make it known that the farmer pays back the money.
We have been hearing a lot about food in these past weeks and I sometimes wonder why it has taken us three decades to realize the consequences of our agricultural programs. It is only three or four years since the LIFT program was introduced. We can look at the bill in that light and see that it begins to implement a philosophy relating to farmers which is long overdue. At long last farmers are beginning to be recognized as professionals, a status which agricultural producers have never enjoyed. Let me ask, why were farm people not represented at the World Food Conference in Rome? There, a whole organization was talking about international food production and there was not one farm representative from this country except the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). There was much talk of food production but there was no farm representation.
Although I applaud this legislation as being one small step toward implementing professionalism in agricultural production, I say that we are doing too little, too late. If the conference in Rome had dealt, say, with oil instead of with food, can you imagine oil interests being represented only by the government? Would not one have expected to
(Mr. Ritchie.]
see representatives of the oil industry at such a conference?
This bill is important because it represents one small step toward professionalism in agriculture and permits farmers to make predictions concerning agricultural production. If farmers are to be managers of their businesses, they must be granted the right of prediction. Thus, this bill starts to introduce what may be termed as the element of predictability. For example, consider what has happened in the beef industry. Some time ago the Liberal government in its so-called wisdom said to Canadian farmers, "We do not need so much grain. Grow grass." They introduced LIFT, and the results are there for all to see.
Now, because of an excess of beef, we have witnessed on television the slaughter of cattle. This is happening at a time when markets have not been stabilized. This instability has resulted from our interfering with the market system. That is why I say there can be no professionalism in farming until there is professionalism in the marketplace. Production will only be stabilized when farmers can predict market demand. The ability to predict is important if we are to maintain high, stable, ongoing, effective methods of production. For too long farming has been associated with life style and not with business. The farmer has been treated as a labourer, not as one who deals with pesticides and insecticides or acts as a veterinarian, or one who looks after a large capital outlay. The average farm on the prairies is worth at least as much as the average small business, perhaps even more.
This bill is to increase maximum advances from $6,000 to $15,000 per individual borrower and in so doing it seeks to keep abreast of conditions in the agricultural industry. It takes into account cost increases brought on by inflation and the difference between today's production costs and those of 15 or 20 years ago. However, I must raise one question about this bill. The increase provided for is not based on any principle: there is no sliding scale for advances and no formula which will take into account increases in costs of production. I suggest that if farmers are to become professionals and produce great quantities of high quality food, the bill must do more than just set a figure.

With respect, there is no connection between the cost of production and the amount per bushel advanced. In other words, the bill provides for a flat rate. Let me talk about another important area. The federal government and provincial governments must accept an increased responsibility for maintaining agricultural land in production. Failure to do this will bring consequences which will be absolutely frightening in view of current trends. Literally, on every parcel of prime land in Canada we see industrial development and transportation systems.
November 19, 1974

If we were to examine a soil zone map of Canada we should see that land of the highest quality is being swallowed up by industry and transportation systems. I have learned that in the United States about 100,000 acres per day are put under concrete or pavement. Although I do not have Canadian data, I suggest that an equivalent amount of our land is so used, if we bear in mind our lesser population. We need soil and water for food production. If we ignore the importance of these resources we shall suffer the consequences.
Anthropologists say that human beings have been on earth for at least 50,000 years, every day of which men have eaten food or searched for food. Only in the last 2,000 or 3,000 years have we used hard metals, and only in the last two or three generations have we used oil. Yet we allow agricultural land to be destroyed. I suggest that we are much more conservation-oriented on land containing hard metals or oil. We must resist the tendency to gobble up 80 acres of prime land merely to build a highway system which will allow one to make a right-hand turn. Why does the government build airports in the midst of class 1 and class 2 soil, especially as this country, contrary to popular myth, is limited in its possession of really high quality soil?
Finally, it behooves us to talk about deplorable conditions in the grain industry for which the government must take the major responsibility. I am talking about what happened on the west coast. Hon. members will recall that in face of the strike of grain handlers on the west coast the government said, before negotiations had taken place, that it would stand by the recommendations of the Perry commission report. That report provided for an increase of about 61 per cent. The government asked farmers to write to grain companies and demand a settlement before parliament was recalled last fall. Now, grain inspectors who work in the same dust, in the same conditions and in the same buildings say that they will not accept the government's offer of 12.5 per cent. Who can blame them?
Originally, the government wanted to give grain handlers parity with longshoreman who worked alongside. The grain handlers said that if the government followed any principles it would grant them 60-odd per cent. We knew what would happen. Now we are witnessing the prospect of another strike; another mess in the grain industry. If the inspectors go on strike, we shall know whom to blame. Certainly farmers in this country would be most frustrated. But that perhaps is only part of their concern. Another concern must be the whole food situation about which we hear so much. We have just finished a week in which people all over the world have been talking about food. We must take a look at the kind of policies that are being established and the kind of commitments that are being made. They do very little to encourage farmers to raise more either in terms of quality or quantity.
The whole transportation system across the west is in a mess. You can walk from my constituency to Vancouver faster than you can ship grain-and I mean that literally. The average speed at which grain leaves the side postings until it arrives in Vancouver is an average of 4!4 miles an hour. This takes into account the number of stops it makes
Grain
at the various locales, the number of days it sits in Calgary before moving west, and the number of days it sits in port waiting to be unloaded. If you can walk from central Alberta to Vancouver faster than government trains can get there, obviously something is seriously wrong. Perhaps the government might suggest we carry grain out there in bags.
All of that is really to wrap up what I am saying. While I support this legislation in principle, the fundamental thing that must be a part of all legislation is to professionalize the farmer to the degree that he feels a sense of predictability, is encouraged and receives a reward for raising food. Obviously, the need is there to raise increasingly vast amounts of higher quality food measured not just by the style and appearance of the food product but by its nutritive value in terms of some kind of nutritive analysis. I simply say to this government they have a lot more work to do if they want to make the farmers comfortable and have as the end result a whole world that is well fed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly to Bill C-10. We in the official opposition have always supported cash advances. This legislation was first introduced in 1957-58 by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). When it was introduced, the legislation made possible the survival of many western farmers who were under extreme cash pressure. The minister stated yesterday that the main reason for bringing forward Bill C-10 was to keep cash advances in line with the growth in inflation. I am glad the government realizes how hard the farmer has been hit by inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext: I didn't say that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext: You did not hear my remarks.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
The minister must agree that no one is harder hit by inflation than the western farmer. We need only look at the extent to which his costs of production have increased in the past few years. In order to increase production he must use fertilizer in large quantities. However, the cost of fertilizer has doubled and in some cases tripled. In the past year the price of baler twine tripled. We must also look at the price of farm machinery. A combine that not many years ago sold for $15,000 now costs over $25,000. A half-ton farm truck that cost approximately $2,500 in 1967 now sells for over $5,000. Inflation is increasing the farmer's cost of production.
Yesterday the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) hit on the real reason for increasing cash advances. Last year the government introduced a new food grains policy. Under this new policy a farmer can sell his wheat to the Canadian Wheat Board or directly to the elevator companies. However, because of the low initial price of grain, farmers are almost forced to sell on the open market. The minister will have to admit that because of this policy, cash pressure on the farmer has been very great. This is the real reason we are seeing an increase in cash advances.
I want to stress to urban members that cash advances are not a hand-out to farmers. They are advances made on

November 19, 1974
Adjournment Debate
future grain deliveries. The farmer must repay every cent. I have found that many urban members and others from eastern Canada think that the final payment to the farmer is a subsidy or hand-out. That is not true. When the Wheat Board sells the farmer's grain, part of the money is held back. At the end of the crop year the final figure is arrived at and the farmer receives the final payment: it is money owing the farmer on completion of the sale.
Yesterday the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) announced an increase in the initial prices of grain. He stated that wheat is being increased to $3.75, barley to $2.25 and oats to $1.20. It is hard for members on this side to understand why the minister took so long to raise the initial prices of grain. Farmers have been demanding this increase since the end of the last crop year. If the initial price for grain was not so low, there would not be so much need for cash advances. The government has continually played around with initial prices: we have seen them increased during an election campaign and reduced after the election. The formula for initial prices should be at least 75 per cent of the expected prices. In this way the farmer would have some idea of the direction in which he is heading. This has certainly not been the case with this government.
One wonders why the minister chose to bring forward the cash advance legislation at this time. There are far more urgent matters affecting western agriculture. It makes one wonder about the priorities of this government. We have repeatedly asked what the policy of this government is on transportation as it affects the movement of grain. At this time we do not know the government's policy on railway branch lines. We know a freeze was put on the closure of all branch lines until the end of this year. The farmer and the grain companies do not know what is going to happen in less than a month and a half. This lack of policy is costing the grain companies, the pool, the grain growers and the farmers great amounts of money. I can give many examples where indecision by this government has been very costly.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakeroldname: Mr. F. Oberle (Prince George-Peace River) moved
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 CREATION OF JOB INVENTORY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
that Bill C-212, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I cannot help being somewhat disappointed that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) is not here this evening. I know of his interest in this matter and of his concern with the problem that this bill is trying to correct. However, I am sure his representative is here. I should like to appeal, not only to members on the government side of the House but to members of the other opposition parties to allow this bill to go to committee since it is designed to correct a very serious discrepancy in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I have just returned from a visit to some of the more remote areas of my constituency in northeastern British Columbia where it has always been difficult to enjoy many of the services of both the federal and the provincial governments. I suppose it is natural that a member of parliament is looked at, in areas as remote as the Alaska Highway, as a liaison officer or ombudsman, and one should not be surprised if a member from an area such as this is always confronted with problems which he is very seldom able to explain or to solve himself. When one thinks of government from as far away as northeastern British Columbia, it becomes an almost impossible task to reconcile the activities of government with the actual needs of the area. One finds in almost all cases that the activities of the various government agencies work at cross-purposes. The Unemployment Insurance Commission and the services offered by Canada Manpower are a perfect example of this, and my bill addresses itself to this problem.
Even if we ignore the fact that the services of these agencies are available only on a very limited scale to people in remote areas, limited service is totally useless to Canadians in areas such as I have described. First of all, even though my bill does not provide for the reamalgamation of Canada Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission, I should like to say that the separation of these two agencies, if they can be considered separate at all, had an even more disastrous effect in the remote areas of our country than in others.
November 19, 1974

During my travels I am constantly confronted with a paradox which demonstrates the chronic and acute shortage of people in almost all categories of the labour market, not to speak, of course, of the total absence of professional people which is a different problem altogether. I refer to the paradox between the lack of people and the rate of unemployment in these areas, which is usually higher than the national average. I could, of course, use many examples but one which demonstrates better than anything else the serious discrepancy that my bill is trying to correct is the situation that exists in the lumber industry of British Columbia and, I am sure, in other areas of Canada as well.
The difficulties experienced by that industry have in recent days and weeks been the subject of attention by the House of Commons and people throughout the country. We have had proposals to set aside any other business of the House of Commons in order to discuss, under certain rules and orders, the problems of the forest industry, and in particular we have addressed ourselves to the serious question of unemployment that is connected with the difficulties facing the industry.
In British Columbia alone we know that at least 15,000 people have been laid off, even without considering the massive cutbacks and shutdowns in the service industry as a result of the slowdowns. The unemployment rate in northern British Columbia now appears to be approaching 10 per cent. British Columbia is considered to be a "have" province, but I am sure that the "haves" must all live in the lower mainland, in Vancouver, since in northern British Columbia there is, as I say, an unemployment rate of 10 per cent. In spite of this, it was necessary for a firm called Fort Nelson Forest Industries to limit their production to one shift since they were not able to employ 75 people. They did not limit production to one shift because of the depressed lumber market, for a change, or even because of shortage of boxcars or a breakdown in rail service; it was for no other reason than shortage of labour. The shortage is not confined to one category but is apparent in all-skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled labourers.
If you were to travel, Madam Speaker, along the Alaska Highway by automobile, as I often do, you might find the operators of a rest stop or roadside facility unable to provide you with service because of lack of help. If you do not know how to repair your own tire, I would advise you not to travel the Alaska Highway this winter because you might well become stranded somewhere between Fort Nelson and Watson Lake, unable to find someone who is able or prepared to assist you. Several business people have told me they find it impossible to continue their operations, and lack of facilities along this highway will make winter travel extremely hazardous, if not dangerous.
One must ask oneself what is wrong with the system. Certainly it would seem that the established guidelines for the two labour-management agencies, namely, Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission, were designed to deal with these problems and I think that in theory they have. Canada Manpower has a wide range of services. A person can apply for a grant to explore a new area in which he might find an opportunity to work. He can get a travel grant to go to another part of the country in order to find employment. We can provide, through
Unemployment Insurance Act
Canada Manpower, a person's moving expenses to a new location if it is found to be a suitable location for work. We can retrain an unemployed person to help him or her find new skills. We can maintain storefront offices in some areas of our country in order to help people seeking employment and employers to get together, and so on.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission has its own programs designed to help people find new employment and to upgrade their skills. But quite often-altogether too often-in remote areas where there are no offices the two agencies work at cross-purposes. Let me give the House an example. Yesterday I telephoned the regional office about a constituent who found himself chocked and buried by a mountain of red tape. When I explained to the regional officer the claimant's case and he gave me a ruling, I said to him, "Would you allow your mind for one moment to be exposed to reason and would you tell me if you think your ruling makes any sense at all, looking at it from the claimant's point of view?" His reply to me was, "Mr. Oberle, I would rather not comment on that". I hope he will not want to comment on it because no one in his right mind could make sense out of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which would better be called "Catch 22".
[DOT] (mo)
This is what happened. The man consulted the Manpower and Unemployment Insurance offices before he left his employment on September 5. He was allowed to leave to attend a school sponsored by Canada Manpower at which he wanted to upgrade himself. He was told he would have an additional three-week waiting period, which he was prepared to accept, so in total he would have to wait five weeks before drawing unemployment insurance. The Manpower course was cancelled after he had given his employer notice and lived up to that commitment. He then started looking for work, but in his field-exploration for petroleum and natural gas-the employment scope is limited. I suggest it will be more limited as a result of last night's budget, since most of the companies carrying out this activity have left the country. As a result of this man's honesty in stating on his weekly report card that he was not taking the training-not because he did not want to; and he quit his job to do so-he is not eligible for unemployment insurance and is now living off his neighbours.
Perhaps that little example illustrates some of the things my bill attempts to correct. Let me discuss in more specific terms the bill I have proposed. On November 22, 1973, in a statement to the Standing Committee on Manpower and Immigration the minister said:
The heart of any employment service is the technique it uses to match job orders with available workers.
In Canada, we have used, and used well, the traditional approach to job matching followed by other advanced industrial countries, seeking from employers their job vacancies and registering Canadian workers by occupation. The match is then made between the two by comparing occupational codes. Our level of employer patronage, referrals to jobs and placements compare very well with those of other countries. However, this approach has not kept pace with the growing complexity of the labour market, and the growing adaptability and mobility of Canadian workers.
The minister admitted we have a special problem because in that statement he said:

November 19, 1974
Unemployment Insurance Act
The current paradox in Canada of high unemployment and increasing labour shortages indicates that employers, as well as workers, may have special problems.
We have special problems and there is no way, in Canada today, that we can carry out the commitment the minister made in his statement to the committee. There is no way we can effectively match employees with job vacancies. My bill would correct that situation by making it compulsory for employers to list with Canada Manpower services and, preferably, with the Unemployment Insurance Commission, a total inventory of job capacities. My bill would establish, in a compulsory way, a job inventory throughout this country.

speechtext: It is not being done any more.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 CREATION OF JOB INVENTORY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: If the hon. member would keep quiet for a minute he might learn something. I carried out a very interesting survey in the city of Prince George. Interestingly enough, this survey was carried out in the same city where we spend annually $334,674 to maintain the services of Canada Manpower, where we employ-my hon. friend speaks about bureaucracy-35 individuals to do what I can demonstrate is being done there. I made a study which pointed out some very interesting facts. Canada Manpower is only involved, in that area, in 7 per cent to 10 per cent of job placements. Only 15 per cent of employers in both industrial and service sectors normally consult Canada Manpower in respect of shortages of employees. A large percentage of job seekers told the people who carried out the survey for me that the only reason they consult Canada Manpower at all is to provide proof to the Unemployment Insurance Commission that they are actively seeking employment.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 CREATION OF JOB INVENTORY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Oh, come on!

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 CREATION OF JOB INVENTORY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I told you if you would just be quiet you might learn something. The greater percentage of employers would welcome such a scheme as I have outlined and only a small number would object to it. Their argument is that most of the information is already in the hands of one or other department of government, Statistics Canada or Information Canada, and they would not object to an exchange of this information. The implementation of such a program would certainly eliminate all abuses presently experienced. We would know what the true unemployment picture is in Canada, and we would know into what areas of Canada special assistance programs should be directed.
In addition, we would no longer have to subject the unemployed to the harassment of proving they are active-

ly seeking work. If we could provide them, with the first week's cheque, with a list of employment opportunities which would be categorized to suit individual needs, this would provide Canada Manpower with factual information as to the areas to which training programs should be directed. It would also give Manpower officials the information needed to justify the implementation of many other services which the office provides.
I have concerned myself particularly with the obvious argument one could expect from employers, namely, that this would be a further infringement by government on their affairs. This argument was discounted by the many comments I received from employers who stated they considered the unemployment situation a problem which must be faced by government, business and labour alike. Almost all businesses interviewed were ready to make their contributions to the cause.
I can go into-I do this at least twice a month, and often more than that-an air terminal or office of a travel agent and tell them I am travelling from Fort Nelson to Fort St. John, to Edmonton, to Vancouver, to Toronto and to Ottawa and the agent will invariably walk over to his little computer, punch a few buttons and give me certain information. He will tell me that my flight will leave at 16.40, Fort Nelson time, flight 48. He will tell me that I get into Fort St. John at a certain time, leave on the same flight at a certain time and that I will have to change to a different flight at Edmonton. He will tell me that again in Vancouver I will have to change flights, but that I will be on the same flight from Vancouver to Toronto to Ottawa, with a short stop-over of 20 minutes. The computer tells him that and it does not take three hours, a day, a week or a month: he gives me that information in two minutes.
I say the advancements in respect of computers and technology must be applied to some of the more serious problems in Canada today, of which unemployment certainly is one. An unemployed person should be able to walk into a Manpower office, where a person would go to a computer and tell him that his category was such and such. He should be able to say that this person could go from category 15 to category 15A, B, C, or D. If there is no opening in that particular category, he should be able to tell the unemployed person that there is an opening in Fort St. John, Fort Nelson, Watson Lake, Edmonton, or St. John's. That information could be available to the unemployed person in two minutes. But, of course, Canada Manpower does not have this information in the first instance, so how could it pass it on to the unemployed person who must prove to the Unemployment Insurance Commission, in order to have his basic right recognized, that he is looking for work?
