speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 CREATION OF JOB INVENTORY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to take this opportunity to offer you my sincere sympathy in connection with the recent passing away of your mother. She was a respected citizen of my riding and please believe that we are most sincerely distressed by the ordeal that has be fallen you.
I would like to thank my hon. friend, the member of the Official Opposition, who has given us the opportunity to discuss the very important and up-to-date subject of unemployment insurance. It is obviously useless to insist upon the tragedy of those who, for one reason or another, do not have an opportunity to find work and for whom the consequences are extremely tragic not only for themselves but also for their families. It is equally useless to insist upon the fact that the unemployment insurance budget has reached astronomical heights and that any solution which might help diminish its alarming growth should be seriously considered.
Bill C-212 would compel every employer to give the Unemployment Insurance Commission a list of his total job capacity together with the kind of job held by each employee and the employer would also have to advise the commission of any vacancy or change in the number or type of jobs. It is easy to see that this bill is made up of two parts. First, we are asking each employer for an official list of his employees and second, no unemployed person would be obliged to further submit to the procedures involved in finding a new job.
In his bill, my hon. friend refers to the 1971 act which, as we all know, contained a considerable broadening of benefits for those who, for one reason of another, are faced with the impossibility of finding a job.
In my opinion, it goes without saying that the 1971 act is not perfect yet, but it is a clear indication that the government is always preoccupied by the unemployment situation, and it is very important, and I agree with the government on that, the unemployed enjoy adequate benefits so he and his family can go through that difficult period because it is then impossible for him to get a job and to contribute effectively to find solutions for his family and for his own community.
However, Madam Speaker, I believe my hon. friend's proposal has a great defect and I say so with all due respect. Indeed the suggested inventory constitutes a duplication of what already exists. We in Quebec are a bit used to that sort of arguments which may not impress my
Unemployment Insurance Act
hon. friend, but we know people who never miss the opportunity of reminding us that we have two forms of government, that we often have two departments, which in a way constitutes duplication.
In order to apply that argument to the matter now before us, I must remind my hon. friend that the Department of Manpower and Immigration already has an inventory of available jobs to which unemployed people may refer easily enough if they are really interested in solving their problems. For if it is a moral necessity on the part of the government to help the unemployed, one must not believe that unemployed people should purely and merely be content to stay at home and wait for public servants or government legislation to bring a complete solution to their problem.
Both the government and the unemployed have responsibilities they must try to share. I know personally that in the Jonquiere manpower office, in the constituency of Lapointe, such an inventory exists. Unemployed people can be provided with general information enabling them to make active and effective efforts to find a job. It is a new form of procedure. Those offices have been created tentatively, at least in my area, a few months ago only and, on the basis of consultations I had with the director of the manpower office, that solution seems acceptable, profitable and effective at the present time, provided of course unemployed people are really willing to participate and have an opportunity to do so.
I recognize that the solution advocated by my hon. friend is somewhat relevant, but I believe it would be preferable to find a mechanism that would ensure better cooperation between the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission rather than try to find formulas which may be excellent but burden the public budgets and in fact are not new solutions. There are often complaints about the lack of communication between the Department of Manpower and Immigrations and the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
I know the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) has looked at the problem, is seeking solutions and has even found some which, however, did not work as expected.
I believe what the manpower offices now have as inventories is the answer, but that does not exclude my hon. friend's proposal, if the unemployment problem is really not worked out sooner or later.
Second, my hon. friend suggests indeed that the unem-loyed be relieved from having to make any effort to find a job. With all due respect to my hon. friend. I do not agree with him on that. I think that when you are temporarily without a job, you must contact the authorities at the appropriate places to try to get one.
In my opinion, it is unfortunate that the unemployed feel that it is enough for them to register at the Canada Manpower Centre and wait very quietly at home, when they are not travelling or on holidays, till someone communicates with them to offer a suitable job.
If we do not want to erode the desire of the unemployed man or woman to make an effort to settle his or her problem, I think it is important to keep this obligation for

November 19, 1974
Unemployment Insurance Act
the individual to take some steps. I recognize that public servants do not always show the best judgment. Often, they require the unemployed to take absolutely useless steps and sometimes too many of them. With their overly strict interpretation of the law, they often deprive the unemployed of their right to unemployment benefits. Far be it from me to suggest that the unemployed be deprived of their right to unemployment benefits through excessively strict interpretation of the law, but I feel that the unemployed owes it to himself to take concrete steps, in a field in which he can work, to find a solution to his problem.
The bill submitted to us by my hon. friend gives us an excellent chance to realize that perhaps, on both sides of the House because neither party has the monopoly on this we have been traumatized, and rightly so, by the acute problems of unemployment. Beyond considerations of political nature, we are trying to find real solutions. I must congratulate my hon. friend for having introduced a bill that is totally honest, totally interesting, which I cannot support wholeheartedly but for which I feel we can certainly commend its author. It has given us an opportunity, though perhaps too brief, of reflecting again on the serious problem of unemployment. This is perhaps a new occasion to to work together towards finding solutions, for there is no worse problem than that of unemployment. Though we must sympathize with those who are without work, we must above all else work together, setting aside political considerations, and find adequate solutions to the trials besetting those people.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 CREATION OF JOB INVENTORY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that there is a certain sense in Bill C-212, proposed by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle). As the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) pointed out, he would like to match the job vacancies with the unemployed, a problem which has defeated many people for a long time. There is no question, of course, that that is the ultimate that one would look for if one had a perfect scheme, and if in fact people were airplane seats.
Unfortunately, as my friend does not seem to understand, people cannot be equated with empty seats on airplanes because there are a great many more people than airplane seats, even in the region of Prince George-Peace River. I do not think for a moment that my hon. friend, when he reads what this bill would propose and takes the time to think his thought through, would want to establish a gigantic bureaucracy, another bureaucracy, when he is already complaining that there is too much bureaucracy in manpower and unemployment.
A few moments ago the hon. member commented on the reasons given for someone in his office being refused a claim in a complicated issue, where the man quit his job to undertake a retraining program, and something went wrong. The hon. member would only multiply that kind of thing one thousand times if his plan were implemented. I think we must consider the unemployed and we must also consider the problems of an employer who reports vacancies. Let us remember that an employer in a small business frequently does not even know how many people he may be using. He has not got a certain number of staff that he uses at all times.
At one time I operated a small business and often hired about 50 people from the National Employment Service, as it was at that time. Usually it was for the Christmas rush and I did not know too far in advance how many people I would need. I am sure that the seasonal nature of the employment is an important consideration in the hon. member's area as well.
The hon. member mentioned that his proposal would do away with the need for the unemployed person to conduct an active job search because that would be done for him by the Manpower Office. Surely this would be a step backwards, Mr. Speaker. Of late we seem to have come down a bit hard on people who register at the Manpower Office and, for some reason, are disentitled.
The hon. member's party claims that unemployment insurance benefits are a disincentive to people, and on the other hand he claims that we should not require people to make an active job search when collecting benefits. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. I do not see how the hon. member can say that an unemployment insurance scheme should be arranged so that not many people will take advantage of it, and then present us with a bill that would make it easier to collect unemployment insurance without conducting an active job search. Surely that is not consistent with the philosophy of his party.
The hon. member must know that a claimant just does not register at a Manpower Office and immediately collect benefits. Hon. members from urban areas, or areas of high unemployment, I am sure receive many complaints that people register at a Manpower Office and are cut off after a five week period because they are not considered to be actively engaged in job hunting. I notice that one of my friends from Newfoundland, who I am sure has these problems, indicates his agreement.
The hon. member mentioned that Manpower provides 11 per cent of the jobs, but I was not clear whether he referred to his own district or whether that was presented as a national figure. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that is not too bad. When you take into consideration the fact that most people find their own jobs, for a single employment agency to find 11 per cent is not bad at all.
I am sure the hon. parliamentary secretary has a few things to say, but before I sit down I would remind the hon. member that people and airplane seats are not the same things. That may come as a surprise to him, but it is a fact.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 CREATION OF JOB INVENTORY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this bill, but obviously members on the other side intend to talk it out and I think we should correct some of their statements before they do that.
I took the time to cross the floor and ask the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) what his question meant when he compared people to seats. Apparently he was referring to a statement made by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) about how computers work for airlines. Members from the other side have inferred that the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River was comparing people with airplane seats,

November 19, 1974

when what he was trying to do was point out the advantages of using computers.
We know the trouble the Manpower Offices got into when they became involved with computers, but an examination of how airlines use computers to fill seats might be useful to them. If an aircraft did not operate at maximum capacity the airlines would be here looking for subsidies, but the use of computers has enabled them to fill their planes and use their facilities to the maximum.
The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River used that illustration to make things as simple as he could for hon. members opposite who concern themselves with trying to talk out bills that sometimes have a lot of merit. I notice some of them are laughing. I had a private member's motion recently, Madam Speaker, and one of the members opposite, who yelled loudest, told me it was a good bill when he met me later and said he was sorry he had to talk it out. I think we should have discussions on a non-partisan basis sometimes to see if members who do not sit on the government benches have ideas that the government could use.
The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) seemed to think that a Manpower Office that filled 11 per cent of the available jobs had a good record. I have had some experience with the Manpower Office in my riding, which has an aggressive manager and staff who make sure they find out what kind of people industries want. The area is growing very quickly and private agencies have not entered the market yet. But Manpower Offices in general do not seem to know what kind of people employers want. A private agency, on the other hand, keeps an inventory of jobs available and knows what kind of people are required. Some of them are using computers and doing well with them.
The hon. member stated that private employment agencies place the people on the top half of the scale, and Manpower gets the people on the bottom end of the scale. That is not quite correct, Madam Speaker. A company in Vancouver called Hospitality Services provides staff for restaurants-dishwashers, waitresses, cooks, etc. I think a dishwasher would be considered to be at the lower end of ' the scale. This company is doing well because Manpower was not filling that need.
This same company, although it is a private company, as the minister well knows, is willing to work in cooperation with the Manpower Office. Actually, it is willing to pay a fee if the Manpower Office will handle some names. The Manpower Office deals with people who are looking for jobs. The agency I am speaking of goes across the country trying to place employees in various restaurants, hospitals, work camps and so on.
An hon. member opposite mentioned computers and said that we cannot compare airplane seats with people. That is exactly what we are not doing. We are trying to solve a serious difficulty within Manpower Offices and place people in jobs. We want to help the employer who goes to the local Manpower Office for an employee. We suggest that there is a better way of bringing employers and prospective employees together.
Unemployment Insurance Act
Some hon. members on the government side say that the kind of program suggested will entail the creation of a massive bureaucracy. I suggest that that is not correct. Most will agree that in West Germany great expansion of the economy there has taken place with zero unemployment. The program which the hon. member opposite suggests will not work in this country has been in operation in West Germany and, as those who have visited that country will testify, you will not find a massive bureaucracy. It is a country dedicated to private enterprise and it is flourishing. Therefore this suggested program has been proved. It works. It is not one which members on my side have dreamed up, Mr. Speaker. As I say, it has been shown to be a good program.
It is important for us to create an effective inventory for jobs. All I am suggesting is that if an employer is looking for a particular type of employee, he should fill out a card. However, we must make sure that the card he fills out bears some relationship to the card which the prospective employee fills out. Computers are designed to deal with this kind of information. They only fail when the information fed into them is wrong. Surely the government, with all its resources, can see to it that cards are designed so that the card the employee fills out is compatible with the card the prospective employer fills out. I suggest that such a system would be better than the one under which we presently operate.

speechtext: Anything would be better than the present system.

My hon. friend says that anything would be better, and I must agree. In my area, and I cannot stress this too strongly because I have close working relations with the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Manpower Office, government services are working relatively well. I represent a small community of 150,000 people and Unemployment Insurance and Manpower Offices, because of their small size, have become involved in the community to an extent I have never seen elsewhere.
When I was first elected, the major complaints of my constituents had to do with shortcomings of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Manpower Office. I received four or five complaints a day. At that time these programs were handled in Vancouver, in one massive office which was several storeys high, and contained several hundred employees. Now that these matters are handled in the municipality of Richmond, many of our difficulties have ended. Perhaps that sort of thing can be discussed if the bill goes to committee. I suggest that computers could do the job I am talking about now. I do not think my suggested program would require a large bureaucracy. Once the computer system is working, fewer and fewer people will be needed to work the system.
Some hon. members opposite are under the impression that the work load of counsellors in Manpower Offices is staggering. In certain areas the workload is staggering, but the workload of counsellors working in the private industry is not. I am thinking of a company in Vancouver known as Dunhill's. I know very well the two men who run it. One is the treasurer of the Liberal party in B.C. and

speechtext:
far as branch lines are concerned. It has added extra cost to the grain companies and the farmers.
I want to use, as an example, a branch line in my constituency. This is a CNR line that runs from Neepawa to McCreary, Manitoba. Several years ago, because CNR would not guarantee future service on this line, Manitoba Pool Elevators and United Grain Growers consolidated service on it. There were four points served on the line, Eden, Riding Mountain, Birnie and Kelwood. To improve service at that time, the United Grain Growers took over the elevator at Riding Mountain and had the farmers in that area deliver their grain to Kelwood. The situation was vice versa with the closure of the Birnie Manitoba Pool Elevator. They had their customers deliver their grain to the pool elevators at Eden. This happened two years ago.
At that time both the United Grain Growers and Manitoba Pool Elevators asked CNR about the future of the line because they wanted to keep up the facilities. They wanted to make sure the elevators could be kept in top condition. No matter how many times they asked CNR, they received no assurance.
This summer the main Manitoba Pool elevator at Eden more or less collapsed. This meant that the farmers from that area had to find a new delivery point to handle their crop for this fall, as well as their crop for next year. All this has come about because of a lack of government decision as to which direction it will head on branch lines. Manitoba Pool Elevators have now advised the farmers in the Eden area they will not rebuild their facilities there. Instead, they will build a large elevator at Neepawa. This means a haul of an additional 10 to 15 miles for farmers in that area.
Because of the location of these elevators, sometimes close to our national parks, the farmers have to negotiate a few steep grades, which present them with considerable difficulty with their present equipment. The Manitoba Pool Elevators have told their membership, and all farmers in the area, that they will be glad to build a new elevator at Eden, but because the government has not yet decided the future of these branch lines the CNR will not guarantee servipe. This lack of policy is going to cost both the pool elevators and the farmers in the area a lot of money.
I can give other examples where the lack of government policy on branch lines is causing extreme concern in western Canada, a matter mentioned many times before in the House. Instead of bringing in legislation like Bill C-10 I hope the government will soon announce its new transportation policy and disclose its priorities as far as western agriculture is concerned. The government should put its priorities in proper perspective.
In his earlier remarks the minister responsible for the Wheat Board stated that the government was not raising the cash advances because of inflation. I do not know what the reason is, but it does make me wonder. Perhaps the reason is the over-payment made to the western farmers in early June. Perhaps it is the two-price wheat payment that the government is now demanding back from the western farmers.

Perhaps by increasing cash advances the government feels the farmers will be able to afford to pay back the over-payment that was made at election time. Between May 27 and June 3 cheques were mailed out, by the minister's office, to 9,586 special permit holders in western Canada as two-price wheat payments. Later it was disclosed that 7,635 of these permit holders were overpaid varying amounts totalling in all $1,449,000.
At the time the minister stated that the computer had made a mistake, but it makes one wonder whether it was not another form of election bribe to the western farmers. As I say, perhaps the reason the minister is raising cash advances is to enable the farmers to repay the bribe that was made at that time. In closing, may I say I support Bill C-10. However, I feel there is much more important legislation that the government should be bringing forward to solve some of the problems in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board speaking yesterday on this bill, and I was interested to hear him speak so highly of it. This bill is amending an act which came into being as a result of legislation brought in by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was Prime Minister some 17 years ago. Naturally the minister gave no recognition to this fact in his address. He delivered his speech in such a manner as to lead people to believe that this piece of legislation was entirely his own doing.
Of course this is not uncommon with government members. They very often adopt the policies and ideas of the opposition, and later on rather brazenly give the impression that they are their ideas. In particular I recall quite vividly that our policy of indexing income tax, which was brought forward in 1972, was ridiculed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), but subsequently adopted by him.
In his speech yesterday the minister had this to say about the income of farmers, as reported at page 1404 of Hansard:
Hon. members will have recently noticed figures for the whole of Canada which show that farmers' cash receipts are up to more than 43 per cent in the first nine-month period of 1974.
They will have noticed, too, that in the province by province analysis the greatest increases have taken place in the prairie provinces. Saskatchewan leads the way with cash receipts which have moved to $1.93 billion for the nine-month period, from $1.02 billion for the corresponding period a year earlier. That is an increase of approximately 90 per cent for Saskatchewan, over what I believe was itself a record.
Was the minister is charge of the Wheat Board attempting to give the rest of the country the impression that farmers in the west have never had it so good? The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) straightened the record out, however, when he spoke shortly after the minister and quoted statistics to the effect that in 1973 the average income of the farm family on the prairies, after expenses and interest, amounted to some $2,200. I believe the minister is out of touch-if he ever was in touch-with the farmers of Saskatchewan.
I wonder whether he realizes that up until two or three years ago farmers on the prairies were living on their equipment depreciation allowances. Year by year their machinery was getting older and they had no money to buy new machinery. They now have a few dollars in their

November 19, 1974

pockets but equipment prices are very high, having gone up four, five or six times in the last few years.

I would say that the increase in income that the farmer has realized in the last two or three years has largely been eaten up by his expenditures on replacing farm machinery. The price of fertilizer has gone up two or three times, the price of fuel has gone up, grocery bills and general living expenses have gone up. The farmer has been called upon to pay interest on loans at anywhere between 10 and 15 per cent.
While we must admit that cash receipts for the last year or two have been high, it is a case of considering what the farmer has in his pocket after he has paid his bills. The minister will find it is not just that much. Certainly there are some large farms doing quite well and those farmers have bank accounts and so on, but the average farmer has used most of the money that he has received in the last two or three years to update his equipment and pay off some of his debts.
I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) who stated that, in his opinion, this bill became necessary because of the feed grain policy that was instituted last year. This is probably the only reason the bill is before the House.
I assume the minister and the officials of the Canadian Wheat Board are concerned about the possibility that when elevators are plugged, and quotas are closed, some No. 1 and 2 CW wheat will be sold on the open market as 3CW, unless farmers have a fair amount of cash available under the provisions of this bill.
The minister spoke yesterday about a logical and full-scale stabilization program for grains on the prairies. I wonder if this program started with Operation LIFT and will end with the abandonment of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. I am afraid that might be the case, as the minister has been putting out feelers recently, testing public opinion on the suggestion that producers on the prairie will not suffer if the Crowsnest Pass freight rates are abolished.
It has been suggested that the subsidies being paid to the railway companies should be paid either directly to the farmers or to the municipalities for the construction of roads and public works following certain rail line abandonments. Perhaps the money will be put into the Wheat Board Pool account and divided up in that manner. I wonder whether some producers in Saskatchewan realize that if we take off the Crowsnest Pass freight rates this could mean an increase in transportation charges on wheat of from 50 cents to 75 cents per hundredweight. The whole transportation and grain handling systems must be examined thoroughly.
We have received no answer from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to our questions about his intention in connection with rail line abandonments following the

freeze which will end December 31 of this year. A decision must be taken fairly quickly, as the elevator companies must know what is going to happen in order that they can make necessary plans for the construction of elevators and storage facilities. I suggest that the railway companies and the producers must know what is to happen. The farmers must know if they will be able to deliver grain to the local elevator or how far they will have to travel to get their grain to market.
The farmers must also know what kind of trucks they will require to transport their grain, and the cost of moving the grain to market. If the Crowsnest Pass freight rates are abolished it might be cheaper to move the grain to the Lakehead by truck rather than by rail. This is what is happening in the United States at the present time.
Will the full-scale stabilization program suggested by the minister involve on-farm storage? It would seem to me that if we had a type of on-farm storage it might eliminate the need for a cash advance program such as we are discussing tonight. The farmer would benefit by being paid for the storage of his grain on his farm. This would enable him to build modern storage facilities, dual purpose or otherwise, thus assisting him to modernize his farm. This in itself would make quite a difference in the appearance of farms in western Canada. If one travels around the prairies at the present time he will see some pretty poor storage facilities, mainly because the farmers have not had the cash to build new grain storage bins.

It is not because I come from the constituency of Hamilton-Wentworth, which contains some of the most arable land and the most dedicated farmers in Canada, that I rise to speak, because obviously this bill will have a particular interest, not for the farmers of southern Ontario, but for the Canadian grain farmers, chiefly those in western Canada. I rise to make the point that this bill affects not just those members who have the honour of representing grain producers, and not just those of us who represent other segments of the agricultural industry, but simply because this bill affects all hon. members. It is because of the implications of this bill for people from every walk of life and every part of the nation that I speak.
I make this brief interjection in the hope that the debate will not review the bill with the narrowest of views, thinking only of the direct implications, but will take the widest possible view, recognizing that Bill C-10, coming as it does in the particular circumstances of today, is significant for all Canadians and, very hopefully, is significant for all the people of the world.
I am particularly pleased to note that cash advance legislation for our grain producers was first introduced by the government of the right hon. member for Prince
Grain
Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). At that time the Liberal Party opposed such legislation. It is interesting and noteworthy that the government now has turned around and presented this bill, under the name of its minister from the province of Saskatchewan.
It was in connection with my work with the right hon. member for Prince Albert, before becoming a member of this House, that I first visited the province of Saskatchewan to campaign with him in his constituency. That was in 1968. I have been back to that province campaigning with him in the last election. I have also been back to that province, for other reasons, on many occasions. During my visits to that province I had occasion to spend some time in the beautiful city of Saskatoon, which is represented in part by the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, and also by my colleague who has a distinguished record as a barrister, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn).
During these visits I have had the fortunate opportunity to speak to some of Canada's grain producers. I have come to appreciate, to some limited extent, the many difficulties they face. That over-all personal impression has been buttressed by the many conversations with my hardworking colleagues who represent them in parliament, and through listening to the speeches of hon. members in debates such as this.
As well, I have become aware that one does not necessarily have to be involved in the industry to be knowledgeable or concerned about the problems and the potential of those involved in grain production. This is evidenced, I suppose, if one wished to be particularly generous, by the fact that the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board does not claim personal involvement in the industry. This has been evident to me from my personal conversations with his predecessor as a member of parliament from the city of Saskatoon, Dr. Lewis Brand who, although a member of the medical profession not involved in farming, demonstrated a knowledge of the problems facing the farmers in the constituency of Sas-katoon-Humboldt that brought great credit to him and to those who supported him.
One of the most pressing problems expressed to me is the need for stability if people engaged in the grain production industry are to enjoy living in an atmosphere of security. I believe this is necessary. I am glad the government has finally recognized that the maximum amount that may be payable under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act must be increased to take into account the economic conditions facing Canadians earning their livelihood in this way, and facing Canadians generally who have felt the continuing effects of rising inflation over the last several years.
In agreeing with this provision of the bill I feel obliged, as well, to note the fact that we in this party also have some reservations in respect to it. However, these, I believe, have already been clearly voiced by other members of this party who are far more knowledgeable with respect to these aspects of the legislation than I could ever claim to be, Mr. Speaker. What I do say is that in commending the minister for the positive reform this bill provides, I hope he will also take the reservations and suggestions expressed by my colleagues in the true spirit

in which they are offered, and that he and the government will for once be willing to give careful consideration to the merits of the arguments presented by members on the other side of the House.
In the atmosphere of partisanship that is inherent in our parliamentary system and in this business of politics, given the party system in Canada, we face the daily and considerable temptation of allowing our party loyalty to blind us completely to the possibility of there being merit in the expressions of our political opponents. I think we must recognize we all have a common goal, to seek ultimately that which is right and best for our country. So, our approaches may vary, our words may be different and our techniques may change, but our objective, our goal, remains the same. I hope the minister will understand and take this into consideration as he ponders the proposals put forward by my colleagues. This is in keeping with what the late Dag Hammarskjold wrote in Markings:
Without the humility and warmth which you have to develop in your relations to the few, with whom you are personally involved, you will never be able to do anything for the many.
It is incumbent upon those of us who represent the many, the many in a country that is diverse and extensive, and who also represent the hopes and aspirations of the many throughout the world, to recognize that our personal relations with the few, and by that I mean other members of this House on all sides of the chamber, must be developed in a spirit of friendship that transcends all partisanship.
Earlier I spoke of the significance this bill has for all Canadians because of the particular conditions in which we are living. By this I refer to the present world food crisis, which must surely be of concern to every member of this House, and to every man and woman living in a land as bountiful as ours, who feel compassion and a sense of responsibility for our brothers and sisters of mankind. We have been reminded in recent days, from many sources, of the grave implications that the world food crisis has for millions of people. We are reminded of it every day through the media, and by particular events such as the recent World Food Conference in Rome, where my party was so well represented by the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis), whom I know to be a man of great compassion and bearing a sense of true international responsibility.
In the same spirit in which I have made that comment and those which preceded it, I should also take notice of the contribution made by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier). Hon. members are also reminded of this situation by their constituents. We receive letters of representation from constituents writing as concerned Canadians. We were eloquently reminded of the problem during the special debate which took place in this House last Friday, which debate was initiated by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan). I refer to the international food crisis.
The point I wish to emphasize in supporting this contention is that the bill has implications for all of us, rural and urban dwellers alike. In the continuing fight against inflation, which all Canadians have faced and are facing, the

central concern has been the production and cost of food. This is a common concern of all hon. members, reflecting as it does a common concern of all Canadians who, in recent years, have been asked to set aside much larger percentages of their family budgets for the purchase of food.
This is a very serious situation and one of continuing and pressing importance to my colleagues and myself in this party. Indeed, we believe that any attack upon inflation, any general thrust to ease its impact, must first be directed against inflation that has affected particularly the cost of the necessities of life: food, shelter and clothing. I make this observation because nothing that I am about to say is in any way meant to lessen the importance of the need for this government, and all governments in Canada, to wage an effective fight against undue increases in the cost of living, particularly as they relate to food.
At the same time I think it is incumbent upon us, at this particular stage of world development, to reflect upon the great benefits that are ours simply by the good fortune of fate which has called us to be Canadians and to live in this land. Just as partisanship, which I mentioned earlier, must not blind members of this House to the merits found in the ideas of members of other parties, so it is that we, as Canadians, must never let our domestic problems, however great they may be, blind us to the more serious and pressing problems of peoples living in developing countries. It is essential that this government, this House and all Canadians recognize that whatever our problems are as they relate to food, these are small when compared with the daily struggle for life faced by so many throughout the world.
I view this as one of the most serious challenges facing the world today, placing a special responsibility on those of us who are privileged to live in a developed and prosperous nation, and particularly placing a responsibility upon men and women involved in the public life of such a nation. At the basis of any action to be taken by governments must be the understanding and support of citizens willing to show the kind of self-restraint that so many Canadians have unselfishly come to accept in recent days.
My colleagues and I are committed to use all the resources available to us to the end of bringing true peace, justice and hope to all the peoples in the world. This problem has also been recognized by spokesmen for the government, and as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen)-whom I am glad to see in the House tonight-will know, I have recently passed along to him comments in support of Canada's position taken at the World Food Conference, and directed to the government by constituents in Hamilton-Wentworth. I was pleased to read a speech made by the minister at that conference, delivered on November 6 of this year, part of which reads:
-mankind has no choice but to arrange his feeding in harmony with a balanced use of all the earth's resources, or his civilization will go the way of those of Nineveh and Babylon-which destroyed the soils that fed them. The World Population Conference at Bucharest marked the first, albeit halting, step towards using a full range of policies to control the pressures exerted on this planet's resources. Progress in this area must be accelerated.
The spirit reflected in the minister's remarks has been one that has caught the conscience of Canadians in all
November 19, 1974

walks of life. This is evidenced further by a resolution recently passed by the Hamilton Steelworkers Area Council representing a group of men who, I am sure even the minister will admit, work in a much different environment than does he. Yet they too recognize this concern and recently passed a motion which reads as follows:
The United Steelworkers recognize the world-wide problems of hunger and starvation, and condemn any policies which result in uncalled for cuts in food production, or in storage policies which risk the spoilage of food.
This is a problem which transcends all political considerations and all economic differences that may separate Canadians. It unites us all, whatever our background, whatever our walk of life, whatever our aspirations for our own personal development, in a common concern to feel a commitment and to make a contribution to international relations.
This is why I further support, as a general rule, the provision by Canada of aid to assist the citizens of a country rather than the giving of assistance directly to a foreign government. In this way it is possible to disagree with the policies of another government, but not to let those policies stand in the way of assisting people who are in need, and who should not be made to suffer as a result of the shortcomings of their country's officials. A significant problem presented by such a policy, we must admit, is to ensure that this really benefits those citizens and is not misdirected by the government in question. It is in this spirit, with this intention, that any action on the part of the federal government, to provide aid for the people of any country in need, is deserving of our support.
So I welcome this bill chiefly because it should create conditions favourable to high productivity on the part of our grain producers. Productivity, high productivity, absolute and ultimate high productivity-that must be the byword and the objective of every farmer in every part of Canada in the coming years. Never again should we have a government policy, as this government had, to pay farmers for not producing food, the chief among the essentials of life. Rather, we must adopt the attitude enunciated so eloquently by the late President Kennedy when he said:
I don't regard . . . agricultural surplus as a problem. I regard it as an opportunity ... I think the farmers can bring more credit, more lasting goodwill, more chance for peace, than almost any group, if we recognize that food is strength, and food is peace, and food is freedom, and food is a helping hand to people around the world whose goodwill and friendship we want.
It is in this spirit that I welcome this legislation, and express the deep hope that the government will act in consequence of the deep concern which, I believe, is felt by all Canadians for the needy people of the world.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take the opportunity of this debate to present a few of my views on the matter of grain handling and grain production. Before the minister closes the debate I would like to have an opportunity to mention a few of these matters.
Bill C-10 will increase cash advance payments from $6,000 to $15,000. According to the Order in Council that has been passed for quota acres for the purposes of cash advances at 10 bushels for wheat, 20 bushels for barley, and 20 bushels for oats, at a rate of payment of $1.50 for
Grain
wheat, 90 cents for barley, and 70 cents for oats, a farmer applying for a cash advance, if he is a wheat producer, must have approximately 1,000 acres to get a $15 per acre maximum advance. I should like to ask the minister if the formula could not be changed to take into consideration the producers in Manitoba, whose operations are likely to be smaller than producers further west?
Although I believe it was the minister's intention to present this bill as a housekeeping measure, I think it was also a recognition of the increased costs of production faced by all western farmers.
The constituency of Provencher is located in the so-called designated area of the Canadian Wheat Board, but despite this it is also a large importer. Production costs of beef, poultry-and I almost hesitate to mention eggs in view of the government's attitude toward that product- have increased in past years. I would suggest to the minister that he might consider a stabilization program for other agricultural products within the Wheat Board area.
In view of the food crisis facing the world today it behooves us, as one of the few countries with surplus capacity, to produce food so that the hungry people of the world can be fed. The impact of the crisis becomes more vivid when one realizes that many thousands of people in the world did not eat dinner neither today nor yesterday.
The government, however, embarked on a deliberate program of cutting back production, reacting to what it thought was a surplus situation. Operation LIFT was introduced in order to take the political heat off the government, and now we find ourselves not only in a "cash short" situation but in trouble with the beef industry as well. To a large extent the leadership of the government has brought us to this point. It will have to show much better leadership to get western Canadian farmers into a cash position so that they can produce at maximum capacity and help feed a hungry world.
I support the concept of an international food bank to which Canada would be a mojor contributor. But the burden must be shared by the industrial countries of the world, Mr. Speaker, including the newly rich countries of the Middle East which should make a cash contribution toward the creation of such a food bank.
The cyclical nature of agriculture means that it cannot be regularized, and the government should seriously consider giving financial aid to Canadian farmers in order to ensure steady production. It needs to be made clear to the consumers, however, that such assistance should not be classified as farm subsidies but rather as consumer subsidies. Such aid is only available to the farmer to give him a reasonable return on his input costs. This matter should be set straight for the record.
It is possible that Bill C-10 would not have been necessary in its present format if the initial payment had been higher. That has been changed recently, but we still have the three bushel quota which is forcing many farmers on the open market.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to impress upon the government that if agriculture is to remain viable it must be in a cash flow position. Production must be

November 19, 1974
Grain
increased so that we can help the hungry of the world, but it must not be done at the expense of the farmer.

First of all, however, I must observe that we have had another of these fairly typical debates that take place when the subject is grain or wheat. This debate perhaps confirms the wisdom of the suggestion made by the government House leader that debates in this House should be televised.
Some 11 Conservatives have spoken in succession after the first round was completed and it was made clear that all members would support the bill presently before the House. The advantage of television would have been that every set in the country could have turned off ten Tories ago and that might have-

speechtext: You haven't got any Liberals in western Canada at all. You can't restrict debate.

speechtext:
The important thing is that of those 11 speeches, two might have been worth discussion if they had been allowed to go forward because they had some relevance to the subject of the debate. I should like to make it clear that I do not refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan). I appreciate his entering the debate, recognizing as he did, that he does not represent an area which is greatly concerned about the subject, but that he wished to utter important words of poetry and get the subject off his soul.
I thought the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) and the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) spoke well on current issues and, in a sensible and rational way, put forward questions and propositions of relevance. This distinguishes them completely from other Conservatives who took part in this debate. If one thing is clear, it is that those other Conservatives who participated in the debate have not taken advantage of the services of their research bureau in preparing material to be presented in the debate.
We heard two sorts of presentation: we heard the sort of thing we have heard many times previously, that is, hackneyed repetitions of old charges, old comments and old analyses. There was nothing new in them. Yes, there was something new in this debate, and that was the completely fictitious and completely false positions put forward by some. It was absolutely astounding for members sitting on my side to listen to that kind of impossible contribution made by hon. members opposite on a bill which, as 11 members in succession said, they will support because, "after all, we invented this idea and therefore it is good."

Members opposite began by observing that they could not understand how the Liberal government can support cash advances 17 years after Conservatives introduced the principle. They, being Conservatives, think that if you are against something in 1957, by George, you will be against it in 1974. Well, Mr. Speaker, some Liberals who were here in 1957 are not here now. Times and ideas change, and the Liberal party has changed. It adopts the best policies put forward by any side of the House, and does so unashamedly.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) made a number of remarks attempting to show, I think, that the Conservatives seem to be against demurrage payments being borne by the Canadian Wheat Board. Clearly, demurrage payments on wheat, are the responsibility of the board and are borne by the board. Demurrage charges on grains which are not the responsibilities of the Wheat Board, whether on rape or flaxseed, are borne by those involved with those particular grains. He was also concerned about the possibility of the cost of boxcars being borne by grain farmers. He ought to know that these boxcars were paid for by the treasury.
I also found interesting the hon. member's suggestion that the increase in cash advances represents some kind of effort to rescue our feed grains policy. He said that he agrees with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and with the agricultural critic of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Lisgar; he agrees that the open market for domestic feed grains is a good idea. But he was worried in case this bill would undermine that principle. He ignored the fact that when the feed grains policy was provisionally announced in 1973, part of the announcement said that cash advances would be raised in order to assure that farmers are given the choice of delivering to the Canadian Wheat Board or on the open market, as they see best. Cash advances were designed to take financial pressure off them. I mention this to show that there was support for our feed grains policy on the part of the Conservatives.
Then the next member who spoke, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), indicated his tremendous contempt for the feed grains policy and anyone who supported it. Here, again, we saw Conservatives showing their need to speak. Indeed, I suppose they should speak on every issue, otherwise we shall not know how that party stands, as it has not adopted any party policy of any consistency on any subject. It is amazing that they do not seem to know that they take these opposite positions.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) was worried in case the feed grains policy will destroy the Wheat Board. I assure him that it will not.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext: Why do we need it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
We need it because the operation of the federal agency created a different price in one province than was possible in other provinces, and that was unacceptable in economic terms in Canada. We must have one economic price throughout Canada. This should be clear to the hon. member. The feed grains policy will not bring more grain on to the open market than is needed by the domestic market. The limit will be set by demand, and the
November 19, 1974

only relevant question is what price will be charged. Let me say clearly that I believe farmers, generally speaking, will obtain a better return if they deliver to the Wheat Board for the export market. Of course there will always be those who will be attracted by a price close enough to the Wheat Board price to deliver to the open market for domestic use.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext: But only Tories will take the lower price.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member says that only Tories will end up delivering the wrong way and getting the lower price. In that case, why is he worried? The fact is that the domestic price on the open market for feed grains will be close to the basic, long-range price as estimated by the Wheat Board. So, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre need not worry.
In addition to comments on feed grain policy, we witnessed the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) speaking against the grass incentives program. This is the first time I have heard a Conservative speak this way about that program. Usually they voice support for the program, but the hon. member spoke against it. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone) heard him and, not having been a member of this House for long did not realize the strangeness of his colleague's position and spoke against the grass incentives program as well.
I still say that we needed to switch additional acreage into forage, and I am confident in the long-term development of the beef industry of this country. That was the correct program to introduce, as Conservatives at one time knew, but as present Conservative members no longer seem to know. I suppose one can expect no less, considering that 11 speeches were made without the help of research facilities. As members opposite are confused in their positions, all things considered, it might be better if they were to allow this legislation to pass, as most have said that they support it.
The hon. member for Dauphin made useful suggestions, as did the hon. member for Lisgar, concerning the elevator agent as the collector of the cash advance and the administrator of the program. Let me say that I believe the cash advance system has worked so well because the elevator agent has assumed responsibility for an important role. When he is involved in cash advances he knows the farmer he is dealing with, knows how much grain the farmer possesses, and is able to deal with him in a kind, neighbourly and responsible way.
The question arises: is the elevator agent being paid adequately for the part he plays in administering the program? Of course this may involve the elevator agent, the Canadian Wheat Board, and others, but that is another question. We should appreciate the role which elevator agents in this country have played in making the system work as well as it has, Mr. Speaker.
Many speeches, as I indicated previously, just repeated old monstrosities and accusations raised in times gone by-

I want to deal with some of the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). He is the man who manufactured a few facts for the purpose of the debate, which were then used by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) as though they were facts.
It is a most extraordinary thing. I referred to figures for cash receipts in Saskatchewan, comparing the first three quarters of 1974 with 1973. I gave the actual figures and the percentage increase. A few minutes later I was asked

November 19, 1974
Grain
why I had not given the actual figures, which I had done. Those figures showed an increase.
I did not do that to indicate that the measure we were about to put through the House was unnecessary. I thought it would be obvious to anyone that, when a bill stands in my name, it is proposed for passage by me. I indicated it was necessary, notwithstanding that the cash position of the farmers on the prairies is somewhat better than it has been for a long time. I would have thought any member who purports to have come from the prairies, and knows anything about the situation, would know that is a fact.
Those of us from the prairies need not run away from that, even though we may want to emphasize that, despite the fact that today we in the prairies may be getting more for our grain than we would really need to get if we had not a deficit from days gone by, the fact is we have that deficit and it has to me made up sometime. It is being made up very rapidly.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain came out with a fantastic statement which is recorded at page 1410 of Hansard. He said that all the Saskatchewan farmer received for the full calendar year, for 1973, after expenses and interest, was approximately $2,200 per family. He said this is the type of living condition the minister calls "rolling in dough". Of course I did not call anything rolling in dough. I simply referred to the facts.
What are the facts with regard to income? I do not know where the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain got his figures. I ask the hon. member for Moose Jaw not to accept the $2,200 figure simply because it was used by that hon. member. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain must not have been talking to farmers. If he had been, he would know they made a little more than $2,200 per average farmer in 1973.
Statistics Canada figures show that in Saskatchewan in 1973 the net income of farm operators from their farming operations was $993 million. If there were the same number of farmers then as in 1971, that works out to just about $13,000 per farmer for net farm income from farming operations in Saskatchewan.
Statistics Canada further forecast what 1974 is likely to be-it is simply a forecast, but the first three quarters' figures tend to bear it out. It indicates that the net farm income in Saskatchewan for 1974 may well turn out to be $1,801 million. If worked out with the number of farmers in operation in 1971, that comes to $23,404 net farm income per farming operator. That is contrasted to the $2,200 figure of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. It shows what I mean when I say I do not think he has been near a farm in the last couple of years or he would know farmers are doing better than that.
I wish that in the course of a debate like this, improving one measure in a small way, it would not be necessary to have members from the prairies doing several things. It is not necessary to say 11 times over "Let's get on with other legislation which may be more important." Also, they need not once again go over their pessimism about the future of agriculture. If those people had the power, there would be reason to be pessimistic.

We will continue to ensure that farming is a good way of life for more and more farmers in the prairie region and, I hope, throughout this country. That is what this government is about, and that is what our optimism is about. I wish members opposite would share this optimism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we should put on record an explanation of why the House has moved to hold the bill in committee of the whole rather than send it out to a standing committee. If we look at the purpose of the bill, it is merely to extend
November 19, 1974

Canadian customs jurisdiction to the outer limits of the territorial sea of Canada.
It was some years ago that the territorial sea was defined after many, shall I say, abortive efforts and a great deal of promise. We did have a sort of halfway house in regard to our fishing limits. First of all we had a three mile limit, which was then extend to nine miles, a zone where foreign fishermen could come in but our fishermen could not go out. We now have a 12 mile zone and can send customs officers out to the 12 mile limit, and we are determining what shall be the territorial sea of Canada so these officers will be able to operate in what are essentially Canadian waters.
This is a tidying up bill. There is nothing very consequential about it. We are not going to make lengthy speeches or anything like that, so that the shirt tails of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) get into a knot and he becomes overly excited. If there had been consultations, a good deal of the spleen that he vented this evening might have been turned toward some of the scheduling that went on, since Bill C-14 was supposed to be coming up for debate tonight. It so happens that the minister and members of the committee who should have been here to consider Bill C-14 were hauled off to a committee meeting to consider Bill C-9, and were thus removed from the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH AND ENVIRONMENT FROM CONTAMINANTS
speechtext:
The passage of this legislation will mark a pivotal point in the history of this country's response to the challenge of environmental degradation. It is the latest and one of the most important signals that we are passing now from the era of tactical responses to pressing problems, to an era of long range strategy or, to put it another way, we are moving from cure to prevention.
Necessarily our first priority has been damage repair- the rollback of pollution, emergency action to save endangered species, and so forth. These measures have moved forward with vigorous momentum. But we have also been phasing in measures to prevent the damage before it occurs. In the environmental field as in the health or industrial safety field, or in any other organized activity, prevention is always the more efficient and economic way to do things. We must deal first with the very core of the problem. On this, industry and the environmental experts can agree.
Before going into detail, let me say this: it is not being introduced as a replacement for existing laws, federal or provincial. We are talking about a law that will close loopholes, one that will give new effectiveness to other federal and provincial legislation. It will increase the effectiveness of such diverse legislation as the Fisheries Act of Canada, the Arctic Waters Pollution Act, and the proposed act to ratify the international convention on ocean dumping. One of the two key goals of Bill C-25 is to answer questions about chemical substances which are, or might become', contaminants of the environment. When passed, this law will give the federal government new power to gather precise, hard data about substances which may pose a threat to human health and the environment. Where the need presents itself, we want to be able to demand data about existing substances, and about substances that are still in the proposal stage.
Information about the way such substances are used and in what quantity, about their chemical, biological and toxicological properties, is all information on which we will want more data. We will know more about the persistence of these substances in the environment and about the rate and degree of dispersion in ecosystems. We will have a clearer picture of quantities in use. We will know more about concentrations in the food chain, and we will be in a better position to determine conditions of release and control measures.
We need this intelligence urgently. We need, for instance, to understand more about the impact on the environment of phenols and freons. We need to know more about the quantity of heavy metals being released into the environment, either deliberately or unknowingly. Polychlorinated biphenyls, the PCB's, are another worldwide question mark.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH AND ENVIRONMENT FROM CONTAMINANTS

I can give you a lecture on organic chemistry if you like, but this is not the time now.
Although we have no specific law, we have been able to deal with a certain number of these problems through co-operative efforts with the industries involved.
With this new legislation on the books, we can do a much more comprehensive job. Legislation already on the books has been aimed at abatement of direct contamination of either air or water, and has operated by controlling effluents from sources such as factory sewers and smokestacks. However, we have need of legislation that will enable us to deal with the reality that each year hundreds of new chemicals are introduced to the market place, and many may eventually appear in the environment. Although most are probably fairly harmless in the quantities, concentrations and conditions under which they presently enter the environment, there are and will be exceptions. Some need to be looked at much more searchingly. What this act does is to enable us to measure the risk in its totality.
Bill C-25 will give us an excellent new sensory system. We hope it will be an efficient tool. It will require that companies, at their own expense, perform tests and come up with information on the substances to be listed. Following evaluation of the data, the ministers of the environment and health, after consulting with the provincial governments involved and with other federal departments, would make the appropriate recommendations regarding manufacture, distribution, use and disposal of deleterious chemical substances.
The bill will be the perfect instrument for filling all gaps. Without going into fine detail let me say that it is firm but flexible, adapted to the delicate job of preserving the environment.
There is built-in protection against the pursuit of phantoms-of panic button pressing. This characteristic is an essential feature of sound environmental thinking.

In the proposed Environmental Contaminants Act there are provisions for consultation. It calls for mandatory establishment of a board of review to hear objections to measures taken. This does not mean that we must wait the findings of the board before we can act. Emergency controls can be imposed where it seems warranted.
This government, from the beginning of its mandate, has been committed to a balanced view or concept of a healthy environment. The government's policies have been based on an assumption that the physical and economic aspects of the good life cannot be compartmentalized. There is no point in substituting poverty for pollution, particularly when it is entirely within our capacity to attenuate both. An unpolluted, resource-abundant environment, as the setting for meeting human need, is being sought. The vigour and innovativeness of our scientific and industrial sectors are among our most vital resources.
The bill has evolved in close consultation between government and industry. We know the industry agrees with us that this legislation is an idea whose time has come. Many sectors of industry have participated in the design of the legislation itself.
It is our view that it is much better to prevent environmental damage than to go around cleaning it up after it has occurred. We must not see economic and environmental imperatives as being in conflict.
Filtering out or treating pollutants that should not have been in the works to begin with-that is inefficiency. Cleaning up pollution after it has poured into air and water-that is inefficiency too, and very expensive. Trying to revive a valued endangered species when it reaches the very edge of extinction may be a vital task. But how much less painful, and less costly it would be if the problem had been seen from further up the road.
Cleanup does not come as cheap as prevention. We know that the imposition of abatement measures can be economically painful, that it can disrupt established industrial practices. We know that remedies, applied in an unco-ordinated way, can actually complicate the problem. Actions taken to control water pollution may conceivably generate air pollution. Or water pollution controls may metamorphose into a problem of sludge disposal.
Other nations are moving in the same direction-from the cure phase to the preventive. Japan, Sweden and the United Kingdom now have similar legislation, and the United States Congress is in the conference stage with its Toxic Substances Act. With the passage of the Environmental Contaminants Act Canada will have some of the most advanced legislation of its type in the world.
I wish to thank hon. members for their consideration in allowing me to finish my remarks, Madam Speaker.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the short time available to me during the adjournment debate I wish to raise a matter which is of very grave concern to many Canadians.
Since the Canadian abstention from the vote relating to the Palestine Liberation Organization, legitimate concern has been expressed in this country as to whether there has been any serious change or alteration in the Canadian policy, which has always been that Israel has the right to exist within secure and recognized boundaries.
To clarify this situation to some degree I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) on November 12, as recorded on page 1223 of Hansard, whether Canada intended to take part in the debate in the United Nations or the Middle East and, if so, what would the Canadian position be? The minister replied:
I believe that if and when Canada participates in the debate this will give the Canadian spokesman an opportunity to restate Canada's position in respect of the existence of Israel, and its right to exist within secure and recognized boundaries, as the foundation stone of our Canadian policy.
That, of course, is the Canadian position and we welcome the minister's statement. Nevertheless, the stated aims of the PLO give rise to a particular concern. The articles of the covenant of the Palestine Liberation Organization say as follows:
... Palestine with its boundaries that existed at the time of the British mandate is an integral regional unit.
... The Palestinian Arab people possesses the legal right to its homeland, and when the liberation of its homeland is completed it will exercise self-determination solely according to its own will and choice.
As most people know, Madam Speaker, at the time of the British mandate Palestine comprised the complete state of Israel within its present boundaries.
On June 8, 1974, the PLO made a statement. May I read the translated version, which says in part:
The PLO is fighting by every means, and primarily by the armed struggle, to free the Palestinian land and establish a national, independent and fighting government over every part of the soil of Palestine to be freed.
Clearly, the aim of the PLO is to create a new state of Palestine which will extinguish the present, existing state of Israel.
On November 14 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he had decided whether the Canadian delegation would take part in the debate at the United Nations. He answered, as recorded at page 1314 of Hansard:
... I think it is certain there will be a statement by a Canadian representative before the close of the debate. I am not sure when that statement will be made, but it will be made.

That, I think, could be taken as a commitment, in the context of the question and that answer, that Canada indeed would take part in the debate on the Middle East, and that a representative would be making a statement. I point out also that the Secretary of State for External Affairs also indicated that matters I had raised would probably be dealt with then.
When we come to November 18, we face an extraordinary situation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), answering the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), said, as recorded on page 1400 of Hansard:
... no official position on whether we would speak has as yet been made...
I rose on a question of privilege and pointed out to the Prime Minister that his statement was completely inconsistent with the statement made a few days earlier by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Prime Minister graced me with a reply and said, as recorded at page 1401 of Hansard:
It appears that it had been the intention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to have a statement made on behalf of the Canadian delegation, but it was not certain whether he would make it himself or have someone make it on his behalf. If the latter is to be the case, the minister proposes to make his statement in the House around the same time. These were the plans which were laid but they were not absolutely decided upon and it would depend on the nature of the statement itself. The intention was as the minister indicated, but I am not saying there will be no change.
I suggest that the government is involved in an extraordinary state of affairs at a time when the whole world is watching the Middle East.
My question tonight is simply this: Is Canada going to take part in that debate before the United Nations and make it clear to the whole world what Canada's policy has been, and is now, with respect to the continued right of the state of Israel to exist within secure and recognized boundaries which, as I have pointed out, is the antithesis of the aims of the PLO? That is the question I very much want answered tonight, and answered without any ambiguity.

Madam Speaker, I wish to confirm the answers given to the hon. member on November 12 by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). I have stated in this House on behalf of the minister, and the minister stated previously, Canada's policy with regard to the existence of Israel. That has not changed.
