AIR CANADA-PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF BASE AT WINNIPEG-DATE OF COMPLETION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on Novem-

ber 6 was based on a statement made by him during the election campaign in Winnipeg on May 23. The Prime Minister said that Air Canada would build a new maintenance hangar at Winnipeg, valued between $12 million and $15 million, to service its own aircraft as well as those of the Defence Department and some regional airlines. He said this would be begun immediately. It is almost six months since that time.
Questions repeatedly have been asked in this chamber of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) as to when the promised program would begin. To date, there has been no answer.
The question of an overhaul base at Winnipeg for Air Canada has concerned the people of Winnipeg and Manitoba for many years. Looking through the record, I find that my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in 1948, 26 years ago, asked the then Minister of Trade about rumours that Trans-Canada Airlines, as it was then called, was planning to move facilities of all types from Winnipeg, which was its headquarters, to Montreal. He was assured by the then Minister of Trade, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, and the then president of the company that these things would not take place. Over the years, department after department was moved to Montreal.
It is not my intention to go over that whole story tonight. The point is that promises were made by the late Liberal Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson that the base would be continued. During the recent election campaign the Prime Minister stopped in Winnipeg on May 23, and made some very specific promises. He promised that a new maintenance hangar would be started in Winnipeg immediately. He stated that Winnipeg would get defence department overhaul work even before the overhaul base was completed. He said a decision had been made by the federal cabinet the previous week.
The Prime Minister further stated this would mean more than 300 additional jobs in Winnipeg aerospace industry, bringing employment in aircraft overhaul work to a minimum of 800 initially. On that occasion the Prime Minister was flanked by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) and the Liberal member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay).
He said that Air Canada would buy back the hangars sold to Canadian Aviation Electronics in September, 1969, when it closed its maintenance facilities and moved them to Montreal. He said further that Air Canada would immediately start to do major overhaul work on defence department Boeing 707 aircraft at the Winnipeg hangars, and would conduct a vigorous search for other overhaul work that could be performed there.
The Prime Minister emphasized that construction of the new facilities in Winnipeg would not take jobs away from Montreal, a fear that had been expressed in this parliament and in Montreal by various people. The Prime Minister siad; "We're making sure that both places will grow".
These are the promises that the Prime Minister made. I hope the Prime Minister meant what he said and that the overhaul base in Winnipeg will be re-established, will be expanded, and also there will be 800 jobs at Winnipeg. He
Adjournment Debate
also said that this would be done without jeopardizing the work now done in Montreal.
I am realistic enough to accept the fact that what has been done cannot be undone. But the fact is that the Montreal base, simply by virtue of the building on a new airport at Mirabel, will have to be expanded. There is no reason why there will not be more than enough work, from Air Canada and the defence department, to take care of all the people now working at Montreal and all those people whom the Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence promised would find work at Winnipeg. I remind the House that the promise was that the work would be begun immediately.
As I said a few moments ago, it is almost six months since the Prime Minister made that promise. Air Canada officials have said as recently as a week or ten days ago that they have no plans of this kind before 1979. Air Canada is a Crown corporation, and I am assuming it must be responsive to the wishes of the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues.
What I am asking tonight is that the government stop equivocating and trying to hide behind some kind of screen, for reasons I cannot understand. I ask the government to indicate tonight, not to me-what I think of the government is not very important-but to the people of Winnipeg when it will implement the pledges made by the Prime Minister when he visited Winnipeg during the height of the election campaign and made the statement he did on May 23, 1974.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answer to the points raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in his speech of May 23 did make commitments in relation to the Air Canada Winnipeg aircraft overhaul base. I had no knowledge until the hon. member just spoke that this base has had such a long political history.
The Prime Minister did state that Air Canada would construct a new hangar capable of handling all types of aircraft in the Air Canada fleet. He also said that, in co-operation with the government and people of Manitoba, the Canadian government intended to help expand employment at Winnipeg. The Prime Minister stated as well that the hoped for growth of employment in Winnipeg, as the result of the construction of that hangar, would not take place at the expense of employment at the Dorval overhaul base. Employment could be expected to grow at both points.
We do not have the exact date when the base will be completed and operating, but it will certainly be moved forward substantially from the original plan of 1979 as far as Air Canada is concerned. I point out that recent newspaper reports suggesting that Air Canada intends to delay the new Winnipeg hangar until 1979 are inaccurate.
A vice-president (maintenance) of Air Canada wrote a letter dated November 5 to the editor of the Winnipeg Free Press correcting the inaccuracies of that paper's November 2 article. In that letter Air Canada stated that the date of 1976, referred to in the newspaper's headline, applied to

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL-ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO STUDY FULLERTON REPORT-SUGGESTED CONSULTATION ON TERMS OF REFERENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on November 5 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) certain questions in respect of the structure of the national capital as proposed in the Fullerton report, and basically how the final decision would be taken. I asked whether that decision, following the consideration of a report by a special joint committee proposed for the study, would be based merely on a statement or statute by the government of Canada, which in effect could be an imposition of a particular form of government in an area, or whether on the other hand it would be based on agreements which I believe would have to be obtained from the governments of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario and possibly, because there might be a constitutional amendment involved in respect of the designation of the capital of Canada as the city of Ottawa, other provinces. At that time the minister said the decision would be taken by the committee.
I think the matter must go beyond that. Surely the government would not see fit to operate in this very important sphere without at least the consensus I have mentioned. The importance of the question, not just to residents of the national capital, but as well to the people of Canada, can be drawn from the fact that the proposals set forth in the Fullerton report cover the power to tax, to borrow, to plan land use, the question of the administration of justice in any proposed national capital, representation, as well as the whole matter of education, which is a provincial field involving at least two provinces, and the matter of language and its applicability in the institutions of the area and in the educational system.
The matter goes even further than that. If the committee is to deal with the question of the national capital, where it would have to get into the whole matter of decentralization of the institutions of government, the government being the largest single employer, is it to be the thrust of federal government planning in this area to concentrate in the downtown core of Ottawa and perhaps Hull, or is it to be part of the policy of the government of the day to decentralize the institutions of government, bearing in mind the municipalities on the Ontario side outside the city of Ottawa which are capable of receiving government buildings, plants, laboratories and other facilities? This would all have a bearing on the assessments and would assist those municipalities.
All these things are of great concern. It is because of that concern and because this report may influence the decision, and may be implemented at least in part, that we ought to have an assurance now, not just for the people of this area, but for the people of Canada, that there will be no imposition upon the people in the area of any form of government without their consent on the one hand and without the consent of the provinces involved on the other.
Since I asked my question the Minister of State for Urban Affairs answered a question posed by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle).
As I read his answer to that question it seems that there would be no attempt to impose, that there would have to be a will to accept any form of government which might be recommended, and that will could be extended to include the will of the people in the area as well as the governments of the provinces concerned. I should like the assurance of the minister, or his parliamentary secretary, with regard to that point, which is the main point in the question I asked.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL-ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO STUDY FULLERTON REPORT-SUGGESTED CONSULTATION ON TERMS OF REFERENCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member referred to the Fullerton report. I welcome the opportunity to say that I read it to the end, as well as Volume II which includes various appendices and special studies.
I would say I have a great deal of respect for the study. Mr. Douglas Fullerton is highly reputed. His report shows much insight and a full knowledge of the area, where he has been living for a number of years and of which he is fully cognizant. He also has a very good knowledge of various studies undertaken on bilingualism in the area, especially that by Mr. Weld which in my opinion is extremely comprehensive and shows that the area should reflect our dream for this country. I would tell the hon. member that even a fast reading of the Fullerton report indicates the only point on which there appears to be a consensus is that no single agency can model or shape the future of the area, without active support from and agreement with the other agencies concerned. I might say that the main function of the parliamentary committee shortly to be created will be to deal with the development of the capital city over the last 18 years, that is since its predecessor committee last met. The new committee's terms of reference would be to advise the federal government on various aspects of the problem, to determine how best to serve the interests of all Canadians, as well as those of residents in the area itself. To that end, nothing of course will prevent the committee from making its views known to other levels of government. Clearly, such a committee's terms of reference must include much more than the evaluating of Mr. Fullerton's propositions, that deal only with structures for government. The committee must look at the area's future, in the light of the propositions by the National Capital Commission on planning and the views of both regional agencies dealing with urban affairs in an area covering 90 per cent of the Region, an area outside direct federal jurisdiction and NCC planning.
